label: lem:fixed-domain-comparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:fixed-domain-comparison}
Let $v$ and $w$ be a subsolution and a supersolution in this sense on
$[t_0,t_1]\times D$. Suppose that $v(t_0,x)\le w(t_0,x)$ for $x\in D$
and that $v(t,x)\le w(t,x)$ at every exterior vertex adjacent to $D$
at every time.
Then $v(t,x)\le w(t,x)$ throughout $[t_0,t_1]\times D$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $L$ be a Lipschitz constant for $G$, and set $h=(v-w)_+$ in $D$,
with zero exterior values. The scalar positive-part chain rule and
the nonnegative neighbor coefficients give
$h_t\le\mathcal L_t h+Lh$ almost everywhere, including almost every
time at which $v=w$. The measurable function
$E(t)=\sup_{x\in D}h(t,x)$ is bounded on the time interval. Dropping
the nonpositive diagonal term and integrating at a fixed vertex gives
$$
 h(t,x)\le h(t_0,x)+(q_0+L)\int_{t_0}^tE(s)\,\mathrm d s.
$$
Taking the supremum yields
$E(t)\le(q_0+L)\int_{t_0}^tE(s)\,\mathrm d s$.
Gronwall's inequality gives $E=0$.

label: lem:spectral
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The finite matrix $B_p$ is irreducible and has nonnegative off-diagonal
entries. Adding a sufficiently large scalar multiple of the identity and
applying Perron--Frobenius theory gives a simple principal eigenvalue and
positive eigenvectors; see \cite[Chapters~1--2]{Seneta} for the general
nonnegative-matrix result. Because the entries of $B_p$ are real analytic in
$p$ and the principal eigenvalue is simple, analytic perturbation theory gives
real-analytic $H$, $\phi_p$, and $\phi_p^*$ under the chosen normalizations;
see \cite[Chapter~II]{Kato}. Index reversal on the cell gives
$B_p^{\mathsf T}=B_{-p}$, whence $H(p)=H(-p)$. Testing the positive constant
vector in the Collatz--Wielandt inequalities \cite{Seneta} gives
\eqref{eq:H-comparison}, including superlinearity.

The eigenvector equation gives
$Q_p=\phi_p^{-1}(B_p-H(p))\phi_p$ on periodic functions.
It also gives the exit-rate terms in \eqref{eq:Q}.
For every oriented nearest-neighbor edge $(x,x+z)$,
$$
 \pi_p(x)q_p(x,z)
 =\phi_p^*(x)\mathrm e^{-p\cdot z}\phi_p(x+z)
 =\pi_p(x+z)\widehat q_p(x+z,-z).
$$
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reverse-edge}
 \pi_p(x)q_p(x,z)=\pi_p(x+z)\widehat q_p(x+z,-z).
\end{equation}
The right and left eigenvector equations also give
$$
 \sum_zq_p(x,z)=H(p)+2d-a(x)=\sum_z\widehat q_p(x,z).
$$
Together with \eqref{eq:reverse-edge}, this equality proves
invariance of $\pi_p$ and identifies $\widehat Q_p$ as the time
reversal of $Q_p$; see \cite[Chapter~3]{Norris}.

These walks can be constructed with a rate-$\Lambda$ Poisson clock,
where $\Lambda$ exceeds all exit rates. At each clock event an
independent mark chooses a jump $z$ with probability
$q_p(x,z)/\Lambda$, or leaves the site unchanged. Use
$\widehat q_p$ for the reversed walk. The rates are periodic, so a
common $\Lambda$ works on every compact set of $p$ values. The number
of jumps is bounded by the Poisson count, which proves nonexplosion.
We write $\mathbb P_x,\mathbb E_x$ for the law and expectation with
$X_0=x$, and use the completed, right-continuous clock-and-mark
filtration. Subtracting conditional jump means gives the generator
martingale. For an affine coordinate plus a bounded periodic
corrector, its path supremum on a bounded time interval is bounded
by a constant times one plus the Poisson count, and has finite
second moment. These bounds justify the bounded stopping times
used below.

For the walk generated by $Q_p$, multiplying each jump $z$ by
$\mathrm e^{k\cdot z}$ gives, on periodic functions, the matrix
$$
 \mathcal L_{p,k}
 =\phi_p^{-1}\bigl(B_{p-k}-H(p)I\bigr)\phi_p.
$$
Its principal eigenvalue is therefore $H(p-k)-H(p)$. This is the
finite-state continuous-time analogue of the transform-kernel construction
for Markov additive processes in \cite{NeyNummelin}. Exponential moments
over time $t$ are
a positive principal-eigenvector factor times
$\exp(t[H(p-k)-H(p)])$, plus an exponentially smaller term locally
in $k$. Differentiation at zero gives the mean displacement
$-\nabla H(p)$ and limiting covariance $\nabla^2H(p)$.
The reversed generator has exponent $H(p+k)-H(p)$ because $H$ is even.

To prove positive definiteness of the covariance, fix $\eta$ and write
$b(x)=\sum_zq_p(x,z)z$ and $\bar b=\sum_{\mathcal C}\pi_p(x)b(x)$.
The centered finite-cell equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corrector-vector}
 Q_p\chi_\eta(x)=\eta\cdot(\bar b-b(x)),\qquad
 \sum_{\mathcal C}\pi_p\chi_\eta=0
\end{equation}
has a unique solution: constants are the kernel of $Q_p$ and the
right-hand side has invariant mean zero. The process
$\eta\cdot(X_t-X_0-\bar b t)+\chi_\eta(X_t)-\chi_\eta(X_0)$
is a martingale. Under the stationary cell distribution its quadratic
variation has mean $t$ times
\begin{equation}\label{eq:variance-formula}
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal C}\pi_p(x)\sum_zq_p(x,z)
 \bigl(\eta\cdot z+\chi_\eta(x+z)-\chi_\eta(x)\bigr)^2.
\end{equation}
By Cauchy--Schwarz, adding
or subtracting its bounded corrector changes the variance by at most
$O(\sqrt t)+O(1)$. After division by $t$ this error vanishes, so
\eqref{eq:variance-formula} equals
$\eta^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2H(p)\eta$. If it were zero, every edge
increment in parentheses would vanish. Summing along a path from
$x$ to $x+L_i e_i$ gives $L_i\eta_i=0$ for every $i$.
Thus $\eta=0$, proving positive definiteness. Continuity and
compactness make the eigenvector bounds, corrector bounds,
jump-rate bounds, and covariance lower bounds uniform on compact
sets of $p$ values.

label: lem:geometry
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:geometry}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The set $\mathcal W$ is a compact strictly convex body with
smooth boundary and zero in its interior. The quantities in
\eqref{eq:pe} depend continuously on $e$, and $\inf_e\alpha_e>0$.
\item The minimum defining $c(n)$ is attained at a unique
$\lambda(n)>0$. The normal speed and radial speed satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normal-ray}
 c(n)=\max_{v\in\mathcal W}n\cdot v,\qquad
 w(e)=\min_{n\cdot e>0}\frac{c(n)}{n\cdot e}.
\end{equation}
The second minimum is attained uniquely at $n_e=p_e/|p_e|$, with
$\lambda(n_e)=|p_e|$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Strict convexity and superlinearity imply that $\nabla H$ maps $\mathbb R^d$
bijectively onto $\mathbb R^d$: the minimum of $H(p)-p\cdot v$ exists and
is unique for each $v$, and its Hessian is positive definite.
The inverse function theorem gives a smooth inverse and
$\nabla^2\mathcal I(v)=(\nabla^2H(\nabla\mathcal I(v)))^{-1}$.
Since $H$ is even, $\mathcal I$ is even and
$\mathcal I(0)=-H(0)<0$. It is coercive: for any $R>0$,
$\mathcal I(v)\geq R|v|-\max_{|p|=R}H(p)$.
Its gradient vanishes only at zero. Hence $\mathcal I$ is strictly convex,
$\mathcal W=\{\mathcal I\leq0\}$ is compact, and $\mathcal I(0)<0$ places
zero in the interior of $\mathcal W$. Since $\nabla\mathcal I$ does not vanish
on $\partial\mathcal W$, that boundary is smooth. Strict convexity implies
that each positive ray meets $\partial\mathcal W$ at exactly one point. At
$v_e=w(e)e$ the outward normal is $p_e=\nabla\mathcal I(v_e)$, so
$\alpha_e=p_e\cdot e>0$. Continuity on the sphere then gives
$\inf_e\alpha_e>0$.

The derivative of $H(\lambda n)/\lambda$ has numerator
$g_n(\lambda)=\lambda n\cdot\nabla H(\lambda n)-H(\lambda n)$.
Here $g_n(0)=-H(0)<0$ and
$g_n'(\lambda)=\lambda n^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2H(\lambda n)n>0$.
If this numerator stayed nonpositive, $H(\lambda n)/\lambda$
would be nonincreasing, contradicting superlinearity. Hence it has
exactly one zero. Fenchel's inequality gives
$n\cdot v\leq H(\lambda n)/\lambda$ on $\mathcal W$.
At the minimizing $\lambda$, equality is attained by
$v=\nabla H(\lambda n)$, for which $\mathcal I(v)=0$.
Thus $c(n)=\max_{v\in\mathcal W}n\cdot v$. Intersecting the half-spaces
$\{v:n\cdot v\leq c(n)\}$ with the ray $\{re:r\geq0\}$ gives the second
formula in \eqref{eq:normal-ray}; the minimizing normal is unique because
$\partial\mathcal W$ has a unique outward normal at $v_e$. Finally,
$H(p_e)=p_e\cdot v_e$ is Fenchel equality at $\mathcal I(v_e)=0$.

label: eq:normal-velocity-derivative
title: Proof
body_md:
At the critical pair the function
$G(\lambda,n)=\lambda n\cdot\nabla H(\lambda n)-H(\lambda n)$
has derivative $\partial_\lambda G=\lambda n^{\mathsf T}\Sigma n>0$,
where $\Sigma=\nabla^2H(\lambda n)$. The implicit function theorem
makes $\lambda(n)$ smooth. For $\tau\perp n$, differentiation gives
\begin{align}
 D\lambda(n)[\tau]
   &=-\lambda\frac{n^{\mathsf T}\Sigma\tau}{n^{\mathsf T}\Sigma n},
       \nonumber                                          
\\
 Dv(n)[\tau]
   &=\lambda\left(\Sigma\tau-
       \frac{n^{\mathsf T}\Sigma\tau}{n^{\mathsf T}\Sigma n}\Sigma n\right).
       \label{eq:normal-velocity-derivative}
\end{align}
In particular $n\cdot Dv(n)[\tau]=0$. On the tangent space the
quadratic form of this derivative is
$$
 \lambda\left(\tau^{\mathsf T}\Sigma\tau
       -\frac{(n^{\mathsf T}\Sigma\tau)^2}{n^{\mathsf T}\Sigma n}\right)>0
       \qquad(\tau\ne0).
$$
This is strict Cauchy--Schwarz in the $\Sigma$ inner product; equality
would make $\tau$ parallel to $n$. Consider the compact set
$\mathcal K=\{(n,\tau):n\in\mathbb S^{d-1},\ \tau\perp n,\ |\tau|=1\}$.
The displayed quadratic form is continuous and strictly positive on
$\mathcal K$, because $\lambda(n)$ and $\nabla^2H(\lambda(n)n)$ are
continuous. Its minimum and maximum on $\mathcal K$ are therefore numbers
$0<c_0\le C_0<\infty$, which gives the uniform tangent-space bounds. Differentiating $c(n)=n\cdot v(n)$
therefore gives
\begin{equation*}                                 
 v(n)=c(n)n+\nabla_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}c(n),\qquad
 \nabla^2_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}c+cI=Dv|_{n^\perp}.
\end{equation*}
Here $\nabla_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}$ and $\nabla^2_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}$ denote
the gradient and Hessian for the unit sphere, and $I$ is the identity on
$n^\perp$. The first identity uses $n\cdot Dv=0$; the second follows by
taking the tangential part of its derivative.

Lemma~\ref{lem:geometry} already gives a bijection between the radial
and normal parametrizations of $\partial\mathcal W$. Formula
\eqref{eq:normal-velocity-derivative} makes the normal parametrization
a local diffeomorphism. Radial projection is also a local
diffeomorphism on this boundary, since $n\cdot v(n)=c(n)>0$.
Thus $E$ is a smooth diffeomorphism. In particular all quantities
$e\mapsto p_e$, $\alpha_e$, and $w(e)$ are smooth.

Fix $e$ and write $n_0=n_e$. The nonnegative function
$f_e(n)=c(n)-n\cdot v_e$ vanishes only at $n_0$. Its first derivative
there is zero and its spherical Hessian there equals
$\nabla^2_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}c(n_0)+c(n_0)I$.
By the preceding tangent-space estimate, the spherical Hessian of $f_e$ at
$n_e$ has eigenvalues in a fixed interval $[c_0,C_0]$, independently of $e$.
Continuity of this Hessian in $(e,n)$ provides $\delta>0$ and constants
$0<c_1<C_1$ such that
$c_1|n-n_e|^2\le f_e(n)\le C_1|n-n_e|^2$ whenever
$|n-n_e|<\delta$. On the compact set
$\{(e,n)\in\mathbb S^{d-1}\times\mathbb S^{d-1}:|n-n_e|\ge\delta\}$,
$f_e(n)>0$ because $n_e$ is the unique supporting normal; hence its minimum
there is positive. Since $\lambda(n)$ is continuous and has positive minimum
and finite maximum on the sphere, multiplying these estimates by
$\lambda(n)$ proves \eqref{eq:quadratic-support-gap}.

Since $\min_n H(p(n))>0$, the right-hand sides defining
$\mathcal O_t(C)$ are positive for large $t$. Its radial function is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:radial-minimum}
 r_t(e)=\min_{n\cdot e>0}
 \left\{t\frac{c(n)}{n\cdot e}
       -\frac{\kappa_d\log t-C}{\lambda(n)n\cdot e}\right\}.
\end{equation}
There is $c_0>0$, independent of $e$ and all sufficiently large $t$,
such that no minimizer in \eqref{eq:radial-minimum} satisfies
$0<n\cdot e<c_0$: on that region the quotient is larger than the value
obtained by testing $n_e$. On the compact set $n\cdot e\ge c_0$, put
$L_t=\kappa_d\log t-C$ and $d_e(n)=1/(\lambda(n)n\cdot e)$.
The difference from the value at $n_e$ in \eqref{eq:radial-minimum}
is
$$
 t\left(\frac{c(n)}{n\cdot e}-w(e)\right)
       -L_t\bigl(d_e(n)-d_e(n_e)\bigr).
$$
The first parenthesis is bounded below by a positive constant times
$|n-n_e|^2$, by \eqref{eq:quadratic-support-gap}; the second has
absolute value at most $C|n-n_e|$. At a minimizing normal the
difference is nonpositive, hence $|n-n_e|\leq C_C\log t/t$.
Substituting $|n-n_e|\leq C_C\log t/t$ and using the quadratic upper
bound obtained from \eqref{eq:quadratic-support-gap} on the compact set
$n\cdot e\geq c_0$ changes the value in \eqref{eq:radial-minimum} by at most
$C_C(\log t)^2/t$. The value at $n_e$ is exactly
the three displayed terms in \eqref{eq:radial-support-expansion}.
This proves the theorem.

label: lem:Markov-estimates
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Markov-estimates}
The following estimates hold uniformly for $p\in\mathcal P$ and
the starting site.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The transition probabilities of $Q_p$ and $\widehat Q_p$
are bounded by $C(1+t)^{-d/2}$.
\item For each fixed $D\geq0$ and all sufficiently large $t$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing}
 \mathbb P_x(Y_t\leq-D-r)\geq\frac25-
                  \frac{C_D(1+r_+)}{\sqrt t},\qquad r\in\mathbb R,
\end{equation}
and
$$
 \mathbb P_x(Y_t\ge D+r)\ge\frac25-
                  \frac{C_D(1+r_+)}{\sqrt t},\qquad r\in\mathbb R.
$$
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: eq:bloch-kernel-formula
title: Proof
body_md:
We use a finite-cell Bloch representation \cite{Kuchment} and keep
the estimates uniform on $\mathcal P$.
Take the Bloch parameter in
$\mathcal B=\prod_i[-\pi/L_i,\pi/L_i]$, with opposite faces
identified. For a vector $f$ indexed by $\mathcal C$, define the Bloch matrix
$$
 (A_p(k)f)(r)=\sum_{|z|_1=1}q_p(r,z)
       \bigl(e^{\mathrm i k\cdot z}f(r+z)-f(r)\bigr),
$$
where the argument of $f$ is reduced modulo $\Gamma$. The transition
kernel is given by the finite-cell inverse Fourier formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bloch-kernel-formula}
 P_t^{Q_p}(x,y)=\frac{|\mathcal C|}{(2\pi)^d}
   \int_{\mathcal B} e^{\mathrm i k\cdot(x-y)}
       [e^{tA_p(k)}]_{r_x,r_y}\,\mathrm d k,
 \qquad r_x=x\bmod\Gamma,\quad r_y=y\bmod\Gamma.
\end{equation}
Indeed the integral at $t=0$ is $\1_{\{x=y\}}$ by Fourier orthogonality
on $\Gamma$, and applying $Q_p$ in $x$ differentiates the matrix exponential.
The resulting bounded solution is unique by
Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed-domain-comparison}. Near zero, the principal eigenvalue
of $A_p(k)$ is
$$
 H(p-\mathrm i k)-H(p)=-\mathrm i v_p\cdot k-\tfrac12 k^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_p k
                         +O(|k|^3).
$$
Its eigenprojection is analytic and uniformly bounded; all the other
eigenvalues have real parts bounded above by a negative constant near
zero. Away from zero on this torus the whole spectrum has negative real
part. Indeed, if an eigenvalue had real part zero, choose a component
of an eigenvector with maximal modulus. Equality in the real-part
inequality forces every Bloch-weighted neighboring value to equal
that component. Irreducibility propagates this equality along all
edges. A path with net displacement $L_i e_i$ then forces
$\mathrm e^{\mathrm i k_iL_i}=1$ for all $i$. This is the zero point of the torus.
We choose the uniform spectral gaps in two stages. At $k=0$, the
nonprincipal spectrum is bounded to the left of $-4\eta$ for some
$\eta>0$, uniformly in $p\in\mathcal P$. Fix $\delta>0$ small enough
that, for $|k|\leq\delta$, this spectrum stays to the left of $-2\eta$
and the principal eigenvalue has real part greater than $-\eta/2$
and at most $-c|k|^2$, as follows from the uniform expansion above.
If the cell has one site, the complementary subspace is empty and
this part is omitted. On the remaining compact set $|k|\geq\delta$
in the Bloch torus, the full spectral bound is at most $-\eta_1<0$.

The matrices have uniformly bounded norm. Near zero, choose a fixed
rectangular contour $\mathcal G$ enclosing only the complementary
spectrum, with right edge $\operatorname{Re}z=-\eta$ and the other
edges outside a common bound for the spectra. If $P^\perp_p(k)$ is
the complementary spectral projection, the Dunford formula gives
$$
 e^{tA_p(k)}P^\perp_p(k)=\frac1{2\pi\mathrm i}
 \int_{\mathcal G}e^{tz}(zI-A_p(k))^{-1}P^\perp_p(k)\,dz.
$$
The resolvent is uniformly bounded on the compact parameter and
contour sets, so this term is bounded by $Ce^{-\eta t}$. Away from
zero, a second fixed contour with right edge
$\operatorname{Re}z=-\eta_1/2$ gives
$\|e^{tA_p(k)}\|\leq Ce^{-\eta_1t/2}$ in the same way.
For the principal mode near zero, the real part of the exponent is
at most $-c|k|^2$, so
$\int_{|k|\le\delta}e^{-ct|k|^2}dk\le Ct^{-d/2}$. This proves the kernel
bound for $Q_p$. Since $B_{-p}=B_p^{\mathsf T}$, the positive eigenvector of
$B_{-p}$ is proportional to $\phi_p^*$ and hence
$\widehat Q_p=Q_{-p}$; because $-p\in\mathcal P$, the identical estimates
hold for $\widehat Q_p$.

For the scalar projection, use the finite-cell matrix with jump factors
$\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta p\cdot z}$. Multiplication at the endpoints by
$\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta\chi_p^\pm}$ includes the bounded corrector.
The preceding expansion implies, for some uniform $\delta,c,C>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:char-small}
 |\mathbb E_x\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta Y_t}|
       \leq C\mathrm e^{-ct\theta^2}+C\mathrm e^{-ct}
       \qquad(|\theta|\leq\delta).
\end{equation}
Fix $\theta$ in a bounded set and insert $\theta/\sqrt t$ into the
finite-cell characteristic matrix. The principal exponent equals
$-\sigma_p^2\theta^2/2+O(|\theta|^3/\sqrt t)$ and the remaining spectral
modes are $O(e^{-ct})$, uniformly in $p\in\mathcal P$ and the initial cell,
where $\sigma_p^2=p^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_pp$ is bounded above and away from
zero. Hence
$\mathbb E_x e^{\mathrm i\theta Y_t/\sqrt t}\to
 e^{-\sigma_p^2\theta^2/2}$ uniformly on bounded $\theta$-sets. L\'evy's
continuity theorem \cite[Section~26]{Billingsley} then gives convergence of
$Y_t/\sqrt t$ to the centered normal law with variance $\sigma_p^2$.
Uniformity follows by contradiction: from any violating sequence one may
extract $p_k\to p$ and a fixed initial residue, after which the preceding
characteristic-function convergence and L\'evy's theorem give the claimed
limit.

We also need a concentration estimate for intervals. There is a nonnegative
integrable function $g$, with Fourier transform supported in $[-\delta,\delta]$,
which is bounded below by a positive constant on $[-1,1]$ after a
fixed rescaling; for example take a rescaled square of
$\sin s/s$. Applying its translate and rescaling to an interval $J$
of length $\ell$ and using Fourier inversion and
\eqref{eq:char-small} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:concentration}
 \sup_J\mathbb P_x(Y_t\in J)\leq C(1+\ell)t^{-1/2},\qquad t\geq1.
\end{equation}
For lengths below a fixed constant, enlarge the interval to that
constant; for larger lengths rescale $g$, so its Fourier support stays
inside $[-\delta,\delta]$. The Fourier integral is bounded by
$C(1+\ell)\int_{-\delta}^{\delta}(\mathrm e^{-ct\theta^2}+\mathrm e^{-ct})\mathrm d\theta$.
This proves \eqref{eq:concentration} for all $p\in\mathcal P$.
The limiting normal variances stay in a fixed positive compact
interval. Uniform convergence of the distribution functions near
zero, together with $-D/\sqrt t\to0$, therefore gives
$\mathbb P_x(Y_t\le-D)\ge9/20$ for all sufficiently large $t$.
If $r>0$, subtracting the concentration
bound \eqref{eq:concentration} for the interval $[-D-r,-D]$ gives
\eqref{eq:crossing}; if $r\le0$, the event
$\{Y_t\le-D\}$ is contained in $\{Y_t\le-D-r\}$. Replacing the
characteristic parameter $\theta$ by $-\theta$ in the preceding
characteristic-function and concentration calculations gives the stated
upper-tail estimate.

label: lem:mass-decay
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:mass-decay}
The mass $M(t)=\sum_xW(t,x)$ satisfies $M(t)\leq C(1+t)^{-1/2}$.
head: environment

label: eq:M-derivative
title: Proof
body_md:
All weighted moments used below are finite on bounded time intervals.
Indeed, choose $\varepsilon>\sup_{p\in\mathcal P}|p|_\infty+1$ in
\eqref{eq:global-exponential-bound}. Then every sum obtained below by
multiplying $u(t,x)$ by a fixed polynomial in $|x|$ and by
$\mathrm e^{p\cdot x}$, $p\in\mathcal P$, is absolutely summable uniformly on
bounded time intervals. The same domination applies to $u_t$, since
$|u_t(t,x)|\le\sum_{|z|_1=1}u(t,x+z)+(2d+L_F)u(t,x)$.
These bounds justify termwise differentiation of the weighted sums
and give a $C^1$ weighted density in $\ell^1$ on bounded intervals.
The operator $\widehat Q_p^{\mathsf T}$ is bounded on $\ell^1$,
with norm at most twice the maximal exit rate, so
variation of constants also holds there. Equation
\eqref{eq:weighted-evolutions} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-derivative}
 M'(t)=-\sum_x\mathcal R(t,x)\leq0.
\end{equation}
There is also an unweighted bound
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unweighted-polynomial}
 \sum_xu(t,x)\leq C(1+t)^d.
\end{equation}
Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Estimate \eqref{eq:global-exponential-bound} gives
$u(t,x)\le C_\varepsilon\exp(c_\varepsilon t-\varepsilon|x|_1)$.
Split the sum into $|x|_1\le R(1+t)$ and its complement, with
$R>c_\varepsilon/\varepsilon+1$. The first set contains
$O((1+t)^d)$ lattice points and $u\le1$ there. On the complement,
$c_\varepsilon t-\varepsilon|x|_1\le-\varepsilon|x|_1/2$ after increasing
$R$ if necessary, and the lattice exponential tail is summable uniformly in
$t$. This proves \eqref{eq:unweighted-polynomial}.

To measure how much mass lies ahead of the moving plane, put $L=d+3$ and
$$
\begin{gathered}
 z(t,x)=p\cdot x-ht+\chi^+(x)+L\log(1+t),\\
 J(t)=\sum_xz(t,x)W(t,x),\qquad J_+(t)=\sum_xz(t,x)_+W(t,x).
\end{gathered}
$$
Since $\phi_p^*$ is uniformly bounded above and $\chi_p^+$ is uniformly
bounded for $p\in\mathcal P$ and $x\in\mathcal C$,
\eqref{eq:unweighted-polynomial} implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:negative-moment}
 \sum_{z(t,x)<0}(1+|z(t,x)|)W(t,x)\leq C(1+t)^{-3}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $W=\phi^*\mathrm e^{z-\chi^+}(1+t)^{-L}u$, and
$(1+|z|)\mathrm e^z\leq C$ for $z<0$.
The corrector identity \eqref{eq:scalar-correctors} cancels the drift
in the first moment, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:J-derivative}
 J'(t)=\frac{L}{1+t}M(t)-\sum_xz(t,x)\mathcal R(t,x)
       \leq\frac{L}{1+t}M(t)+C(1+t)^{-3}.
\end{equation}
As $M$ is bounded, this first gives
$J_+(t)\leq C(1+\log(1+t))$.

For a walk with generator $\widehat Q_p$ started at $x$ at time $t$,
its corrected coordinate at time $2t$ is
$z(t,x)+Y_t+L\log((1+2t)/(1+t))$. Since the last term is at most
$L\log2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:Markov-estimates} shows that the free transport
of $W(t)$ places at least
$$
 \frac25M(t)-\frac{C}{\sqrt t}\bigl(M(t)+J_+(t)\bigr)
$$
units of mass in $\{z(2t,\cdot)<0\}$, for sufficiently large $t$.
For the strict crossing, apply \eqref{eq:crossing} with
$D=L\log2+1$. Put
$P_p^+(s)=e^{s\widehat Q_p}$. The density equation gives the identity
in $\ell^1$
\begin{equation*}                                       
 \begin{split}
 W(2t)&=P_p^+(t)^{\mathsf T}W(t)-\mathcal D_t,\\
 \mathcal D_t&=\int_t^{2t}P_p^+(2t-s)^{\mathsf T}\mathcal R(s)\,\mathrm d s
                \ge0.
 \end{split}
\end{equation*}
Because $P_p^+$ is stochastic, Tonelli's theorem and
\eqref{eq:M-derivative} give
$\sum_x\mathcal D_t(x)=\int_t^{2t}\sum_x\mathcal R(s,x)\,\mathrm d s
=M(t)-M(2t)$.
For $A_t=\{x:z(2t,x)<0\}$ this implies
$$
 \sum_{x\in A_t}\bigl(P_p^+(t)^{\mathsf T}W(t)\bigr)(x)
 \le \sum_{x\in A_t}W(2t,x)+M(t)-M(2t).
$$
The mass remaining on $A_t$ is at most $Ct^{-3}$ by
\eqref{eq:negative-moment}. Comparing it with the free mass
transported into $A_t$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mass-dyadic}
 M(2t)\leq\frac35M(t)+\frac{C}{\sqrt t}
                       \bigl(M(t)+J_+(t)\bigr)+Ct^{-3}.
\end{equation}
Choose $t_0$ large and set $t_n=2^nt_0$ and
$b_n=\sqrt{t_n}M(t_n)$. Since $3\sqrt2/5<1$, the term
$CM(t_n)/\sqrt{t_n}$ can be absorbed into a fixed contraction factor
$q<1$ after this rescaling. Thus $b_{n+1}\leq qb_n+C(1+n)$, which
implies $b_n\leq C(1+n)$ by summing the geometric series.
Monotonicity of $M$ interpolates between consecutive dyadic times:
$M(t)\leq C\log(2+t)/\sqrt{1+t}$.

In particular, $\int_0^\infty M(t)/(1+t)\,\mathrm d t<\infty$.
Returning to \eqref{eq:J-derivative} and \eqref{eq:negative-moment}
now gives $J_+(t)\leq C$ uniformly. Substituting this uniform bound back into
\eqref{eq:mass-dyadic} at $t=t_n$ and multiplying by $\sqrt{2t_n}$ gives
$$
 b_{n+1}\le \left(\frac{3\sqrt2}{5}+\frac{C}{\sqrt{t_n}}\right)b_n+C.
$$
Choose $t_0$ larger if necessary so that the coefficient in parentheses is at
most some fixed $q<1$ for every $n$. Then $b_{n+1}\le qb_n+C$. Iteration yields $\sup_n b_n<\infty$, and monotonicity
of $M$ between $t_n$ and $t_{n+1}$ gives
$M(t)\le C(1+t)^{-1/2}$.

label: lem:survival
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The corrected jump sizes and the continuous drift between jumps are
uniformly bounded. A continuous exit has height zero, and a jump exit
overshoots by at most one corrected jump, so
$r+Y_\tau\in[-B,0]$ on $\{\tau<\infty\}$ for a uniform $B$.
The Poisson construction gives
$\mathbb E_x\sup_{0\le v\le s+1}|Y_v|^2<\infty$.
Bounded optional stopping therefore gives
$\mathbb E_xY_{\tau\wedge s}=0$: one may approximate the stopping
time from above on dyadic grids and pass to the limit by
right-continuity and the integrable path supremum. Splitting
according to $\{\tau>s\}$ yields
$$
 \mathbb E_x[(r+Y_s)\1_{\{\tau>s\}}]\leq r+B.
$$
At time $s$, condition on the surviving walk and its cell position.
The crossing estimate with $D=0$ bounds the probability of ending
above zero another $s$ units of time later by
$3/5+C(1+r+Y_s)/\sqrt s$. Survival is a subset of this event.
With $h(s)=\mathbb P_x(\tau>s)$, the preceding conditional estimate gives
$$
 h(2s)\leq\frac35h(s)+\frac{C(1+r+B)}{\sqrt s}.
$$
Fix $s_0$ large enough for the displayed recurrence and set
$s_n=2^ns_0$ and $b_n=\sqrt{s_n}\,h(s_n)$. Multiplying the recurrence by
$\sqrt{2s_n}$ yields
$$
 b_{n+1}\le \frac{3\sqrt2}{5}b_n+C(1+r+B).
$$
Since $3\sqrt2/5<1$, iteration gives
$b_n\le C(1+r+B)$ uniformly in $n$. Monotonicity of $h$ then interpolates
between consecutive $s_n$ and proves \eqref{eq:survival}; increasing $C$
covers $0<t<s_0$.
The conditioning uses the Markov property of the pair consisting
of the height and the cell position.

label: lem:killed-kernel-upper
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is enough to consider $T=t-s\ge3$; bounded $T$ is absorbed by
increasing $C$. Divide the backward time interval into three pieces of
length $T/3$. Killing can
only decrease the kernel. On the middle piece Lemma~\ref{lem:Markov-estimates}
gives the whole-space bound $CT^{-d/2}$.

We prove both assertions at once, taking $\chi=0$ for the first.
For the first piece, start the $Q_p$-walk at $x$ at physical time $t$.
Write $a_x=d^\chi_{p,b}(t,x)>0$ and
$C_-=\|\chi-\chi_p^-\|_\infty$. Along backward time $\rho$,
$$
 d^\chi_{p,b}(t-\rho,X_\rho)
 =a_x+Y_\rho+
    (\chi-\chi_p^-)(X_\rho)-(\chi-\chi_p^-)(x).
$$
Thus survival of this path implies $a_x+2C_-+Y_\rho>0$ at every
earlier time. Lemma~\ref{lem:survival} gives
$$
 \sum_z\mathsf K_{p,\chi}(t-T/3,t;x,z)
 \le C(1+a_x)T^{-1/2}.
$$

To bound the last piece, reverse the paths. The total exit rates
agree at each vertex:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equal-exit-rates}
 \Lambda_p(z):=\sum_{|b|_1=1}q_p(z,b)
       =h+2d-a(z)=\sum_{|b|_1=1}\widehat q_p(z,b).
\end{equation}
Both equalities follow from the right and left cell eigenvector
equations. A path through $z_0,\ldots,z_m$ at ordered jump times
$0=\rho_0<\rho_1<\cdots<\rho_m<\rho_{m+1}=T$ has density
$$
 \exp\!\left[-\sum_{i=0}^m
        \Lambda_p(z_i)(\rho_{i+1}-\rho_i)\right]
       \prod_{i=1}^m q_p(z_{i-1},z_i-z_{i-1}).
$$
Reversal preserves its holding factor by \eqref{eq:equal-exit-rates};
\eqref{eq:reverse-edge} makes the ratio of the jump products
$\pi_p(z_m)/\pi_p(z_0)$. Summing over paths, including the path with no
jump, therefore gives
$$
 \pi_p(x)\mathsf K_{p,\chi}(s,t;x,y)
   =\pi_p(y)\widehat{\mathsf K}^{\,\to}_{p,\chi}(s,t;y,x),
$$
where $\widehat{\mathsf K}^{\,\to}_{p,\chi}$ is the kernel of the
$\widehat Q_p$-walk run from physical time $s$ to $t$, killed when
$d^\chi_{p,b}(s+\rho,X_\rho)\le0$.
Reversal preserves the space--time survival condition. The number
of jumps is almost surely finite, and a jump occurs at any prescribed
boundary-deletion time with probability zero.

At the earlier endpoint put $a_y=d^\chi_{p,b}(s,y)>0$ and
$C_+=\|\chi-\chi_p^+\|_\infty$. The forward corrected height is
$a_y+Y_\rho+(\chi-\chi_p^+)(X_\rho)-(\chi-\chi_p^+)(y)$,
where the centered martingale now has drift term $-h\rho$.
Its survival is bounded by survival from height $a_y+2C_+$.
Since $\pi_p$ is uniformly bounded above and below,
Lemma~\ref{lem:survival} and the reversal identity give
$$
 \sum_z\mathsf K_{p,\chi}(s,s+T/3;z,y)
 \le C(1+a_y)T^{-1/2}.
$$
The Chapman--Kolmogorov decomposition has two intermediate site sums.
Bounding its middle kernel by $CT^{-d/2}$ leaves exactly the first row
sum and the last column sum estimated above. Their product proves
\eqref{eq:corrected-killed-kernel-upper}. Taking $\chi=0$ proves
\eqref{eq:killed-kernel-upper}. All constants depend on $\chi$ only
through $C_0$ and the already uniform corrector bounds.

label: eq:stopping-domain
title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:mass-decay} supplies the weighted-mass decay used below.
Fix a sufficiently large observation time $t$ and a site $x$ with
$z_0=p\cdot x-ht+\kappa_d\log t\geq0$.
Choose $C_0=1+\sup_{p,x}|\chi_p^-(x)|$. Run the walk with generator
$Q_p$ backward from $(t,x)$, and stop it at time $t/2$ or at the first
exit from
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stopping-domain}
 p\cdot X_s-h(t-s)+\chi^-(X_s)+\kappa_d\log t+C_0>0.
\end{equation}
The expression on the left is $r+Y_s$, with
$r=z_0+\chi^-(x)+C_0\in[1,z_0+2C_0]$.
The term $\log t$ is fixed during this stopped evolution.

The exponential estimate \eqref{eq:global-exponential-bound} first
places $w$ in $\ell^\infty$ on each bounded time interval. Its equation,
whose generator has bounded rates, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed-domain-comparison} give
$w(s)\le P_s^{Q_p}w(0)$ and hence
$\|w(s)\|_\infty\le\|w(0)\|_\infty$.
For the space--time function $f(\rho,z)=w(t-\rho,z)$,
$$
 (\partial_\rho+Q_p)f(\rho,z)
       =-w_t(t-\rho,z)+Q_pw(t-\rho,z)\ge0.
$$
The Poisson construction makes $w(t-\rho,X_\rho)$ a bounded
submartingale. Apply bounded optional stopping at the exit time
truncated by $t/2$.
At an exit from \eqref{eq:stopping-domain}, the corrected
height is between $-B$ and zero. Consequently
$p\cdot X_s-h(t-s)\leq-\kappa_d\log t+C$, and $u\leq1$ gives
$w(t-s,X_s)\leq Ct^{-\kappa_d}$.
On survival to $t/2$, the endpoint value is bounded by
$\|w(t/2)\|_\infty$. Since $w_t\le Q_pw$,
$w(t/2)\le P_{t/4}^{Q_p}w(t/4)$. The kernel estimate in
Lemma~\ref{lem:Markov-estimates}, the uniform lower bound on $\pi_p$,
and Lemma~\ref{lem:mass-decay} give
$$
 \|w(t/2)\|_\infty
 \leq Ct^{-d/2}\sum_yw(t/4,y)
 \leq Ct^{-d/2}M(t/4)\leq Ct^{-(d+1)/2}.
$$
Combining these exit and endpoint estimates with
Lemma~\ref{lem:survival} yields
$$
 w(t,x)\leq Ct^{-\kappa_d}
       +Ct^{-(d+1)/2}\min\{1,C(1+z_0)t^{-1/2}\}
       \leq C(1+z_0)t^{-\kappa_d}.
$$
Undoing the exponential weight proves \eqref{eq:upper-main}.
For $4\le t\le t_0$, the inequality
$w(t)\le P_t^{Q_p}w(0)$ gives
$\|w(t)\|_\infty\le\|w(0)\|_\infty$, uniformly for
$p\in\mathcal P$ because the initial support is finite and the cell
eigenvectors are uniformly bounded above and below on the compact set
$\mathcal P$. Increasing $C$ therefore extends \eqref{eq:upper-main} to
this bounded interval of times.

If $|x-re|\leq\rho$, then
$z_e(t,x)\geq\alpha_e(r-w(e)t)+\kappa_d\log t-C\rho$.
The uniform bounds on $p_e$ and $\alpha_e$, together with
$(1+z)\mathrm e^{-z}\to0$, prove \eqref{eq:ray-upper}.
Fix $x$ with $u(t,x)\ge\theta$. For each $e$, if
$p_e\cdot x-tH(p_e)+\kappa_d\log t$ were larger than a sufficiently large
constant $C_\theta$, \eqref{eq:upper-main} would give $u(t,x)<\theta$.
Hence
$p_e\cdot x\le tH(p_e)-\kappa_d\log t+C_\theta$ for every $e$; taking the
intersection over $e\in\mathbb S^{d-1}$ gives \eqref{eq:outer-body}.

label: lem:longitudinal
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Fourier representation of the first kernel has symbol
$2\sum_i(\cos\xi_i-1)$. On a small neighborhood of zero this is
$-|\xi|^2+O(|\xi|^4)$, and off that neighborhood its real part is
strictly negative. Choose $\delta>0$ so that the symbol is at most $-c|\xi|^2$ on
$|\xi|\le\delta$ and at most $-c_\delta<0$ outside that ball. The inverse
Fourier integral over $|\xi|\le\delta$ is bounded by
$C\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-ct|\xi|^2}\,d\xi=Ct^{-n/2}$, while the complementary
integral is $O(e^{-c_\delta t})$. For $0<t\leq1$, the probability
bound $\mathsf p_n(t,y)\leq1$ completes the uniform kernel estimate.
For \eqref{eq:heat-local}, write the inverse Fourier integral on
$|\xi|\le\delta$, set $\xi=t^{-1/2}\eta$, and use
$2\sum_i(\cos(t^{-1/2}\eta_i)-1)=-t^{-1}|\eta|^2+O(t^{-2}|\eta|^4)$.
Writing $a_n(\xi)=2\sum_i(\cos\xi_i-1)$, decrease $\delta$ so that
both $a_n(\xi)$ and $-|\xi|^2$ are at most $-c|\xi|^2$. The real
mean-value formula for the exponential gives
$$
 |e^{ta_n(\xi)}-e^{-t|\xi|^2}|
       \le Ct|\xi|^4e^{-ct|\xi|^2}\qquad(|\xi|\le\delta).
$$
Its integral is $O(t^{-(n+2)/2})$. The omitted Gaussian tail and
the integral over $|\xi|>\delta$ are exponentially small. This
proves the stated, weaker error in \eqref{eq:heat-local}, uniformly
in $y$, as well as its Gaussian leading term. Strict positivity follows from the following path event: in
each coordinate the walk is the difference of two independent Poisson counting
processes, and the event that those counts take any prescribed nonnegative
values has positive probability.

The characteristic symbol for $G$ is
$\mathrm e^{\lambda_*}(\mathrm e^{-\mathrm i\xi}-1)
 +\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*}(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\xi}-1)$.
After removal of its linear term it is
$-D_*\xi^2+\mathrm i c_*\xi^3/6+O(\xi^4)$.
The multiplier defining $w_1$ is $-2\mathrm i\sin\xi$.
In Fourier inversion, the first two contributions are therefore
$-2\partial_s g_t(s)+(c_*t/3)\partial_s^4g_t(s)$, where
$g_t(s)=(4\pi D_*t)^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{-s^2/(4D_*t)}$.
More explicitly, these equal
$$
 \frac{g_t(s)}{D_*t}
 \left(s+\frac{c_*}{4D_*}
       -\frac{c_*s^2}{4D_*^2t}
       +\frac{c_*s^4}{48D_*^3t^2}\right).
$$
The last two terms are bounded by $C_A(1+|s|)t^{-2}$ in the specified
region. To bound the Fourier terms not displayed above, split at
$|\xi|=t^{-2/5}$. On the smaller interval, the Taylor remainders are
bounded, after multiplication by $\mathrm e^{-c t\xi^2}$, by a constant
times $|\xi|^3+t|\xi|^5+t^2|\xi|^7$; their integrals are $O(t^{-2})$.
On $t^{-2/5}\leq|\xi|\leq\xi_0$, the
Gaussian bound is exponentially small in $t^{1/5}$; the rest of the
torus is exponentially small in $t$. This proves
\eqref{eq:signed-kernel}, including at bounded $s$.
Finally, conjugation by $\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*(j-c_*t)}$ and
\eqref{eq:critical-system} proves the equation for $Z$.

label: lem:moving-halfline-comparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:moving-halfline-comparison}
Let $B\in C^1([t_0,t_1])$ be strictly increasing. Suppose that
bounded functions $q,\psi$ are locally absolutely continuous in time
at each site and satisfy, almost everywhere,
$$
 q_t=\Delta_{\mathbb Z}q+R(t,j,q),\qquad
 \psi_t\leq\Delta_{\mathbb Z}\psi+R(t,j,\psi),
$$
where $R$ is measurable in time and uniformly Lipschitz in its last
argument on an interval containing both ranges. If $\psi\leq q$
initially on $j\leq B(t_0)$ and on the right collar
$B(t)<j\leq B(t)+1$ for every $t\in[t_0,t_1]$, then
$\psi(t,j)\leq q(t,j)$ whenever $j\leq B(t)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Between consecutive integer crossings of $B$, the interior set is
fixed. Its only exterior neighbor is the first integer to the right of
$B(t)$, which lies in the ordered collar. Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed-domain-comparison}
applies on each such interval. At a crossing, the entering vertex was
in the collar immediately beforehand, so continuity supplies its initial
ordering. There are finitely many crossings on a compact time interval;
iteration proves the assertion, including the crossing times. The fixed-domain
lemma already treats the infinite left end and coordinatewise
almost-everywhere differential inequalities.

label: lem:transverse-kernel
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A transverse principal eigenvector, extended constantly in the
longitudinal coordinate, is a positive eigenvector of the full tilted
cell matrix. Its eigenvalue is the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:transverse-factorization}, so Perron--Frobenius theory
identifies this value with $H(p_1,p')$. At $p'=0$ the transverse
eigenvalue is $a$. Applying the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral}
to the transverse cell gives the evenness of $H_\perp$ and the
positive definiteness of $\Sigma_\perp$.

Conjugating $\mathcal A_\perp-a$ by $\psi_\perp$ gives the Markov
generator
$$
 Q_\perp h(y)=\sum_{|b|_1=1}
   \frac{\psi_\perp(y+b)}{\psi_\perp(y)}(h(y+b)-h(y)).
$$
It is reversible with cell probability $\psi_\perp^2$, and its
stationary mean displacement is zero. If $P_\perp(s;y,z)$ is its
transition kernel, then
$\mathrm e^{-as}K_\perp(s;y,z)=\psi_\perp(y)P_\perp(s;y,z)/\psi_\perp(z)$.
The Bloch decomposition in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:Markov-estimates} applies to this zero-drift generator
in dimension $n\geq1$ and gives \eqref{eq:transverse-kernel-upper}.
For background on the decomposition, see \cite{Kuchment}.
We spell out its leading coefficient because the normalization of
$\psi_\perp$ matters here.
Near zero the principal exponent is
$-\tfrac12 k^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\perp k+O(|k|^3)$, and the
principal projection at zero has entries $\psi_\perp(z)^2$,
independent of the starting residue. All other modes have an
exponential gap. The transverse version of \eqref{eq:bloch-kernel-formula} has
prefactor $|\mathcal C_\perp|/(2\pi)^n$. Consequently its leading
term is the Gaussian density times
$|\mathcal C_\perp|\psi_\perp(z)^2$. The error near zero is bounded
in absolute value by the integral of
$C(|k|+s|k|^3)\mathrm e^{-cs|k|^2}$, which is $O(s^{-(n+1)/2})$;
a smaller neighborhood and the complementary spectral gap justify
this bound uniformly. The Bloch phases from the finitely many
residues contribute only $O(|k|)$ to the projection error.
Multiplication by $\psi_\perp(y)/\psi_\perp(z)$ proves
\eqref{eq:transverse-kernel-local}. To see strict positivity, fix one finite
nearest-neighbor path from $y$ to $z$. Every jump rate of $Q_\perp$ along this
path is positive, and the exponential holding-time density assigns positive
probability to completing exactly these jumps before time $s$ and making no
additional jump before $s$. Hence $P_\perp(s;y,z)>0$, and therefore
$K_\perp(s;y,z)>0$.

For constant $a_\perp$, the normalization gives
$\psi_\perp=|\mathcal C_\perp|^{-1/2}$ and $\Sigma_\perp=2I$.
Thus the cell-volume factor in \eqref{eq:transverse-kernel-local}
recovers the homogeneous heat kernel.

label: lem:product-subsolution
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:transverse-factor-equation
title: Proof
body_md:
The bound \eqref{eq:transverse-kernel-upper} permits a choice of
$\beta_\perp$ independent of $T\geq1$ for which $0<H_T\leq1$.
Differentiating \eqref{eq:transverse-factor} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:transverse-factor-equation}
 (H_T)_t=\Delta_\perp H_T+
       \left(a_\perp(y)-a+\frac n{2(t+T)}\right)H_T.
\end{equation}
The constants $0$ and $a/K$ are respectively a subsolution and a
supersolution of \eqref{eq:scalar-logistic}, since the right-hand
side at $q=a/K$ is $-an/[2K(t+T)]\leq0$. Comparison therefore gives
$0\leq q\leq a/K\leq1$. Writing $H=H_T(t,y;y_0)$ and using the
separation of the lattice Laplacian in \eqref{eq:transverse-factor-equation}
and \eqref{eq:scalar-logistic}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:product-subsolution-residual}
 (\partial_t-\Delta_{\mathbb Z^d})(qH)
 =a_\perp(y)qH-Kq^2H
 \leq a_\perp(y)qH-K(qH)^2\leq F((j,y),qH).
\end{equation}
Here $qH\in[0,1]$ and $H\leq1$, so both inequalities have the stated
sign. This proves the subsolution property with the full local
potential $a_\perp(y)$.

Put $\eta_0=u_0(j_0,y_0)>0$ and fix any $T\geq1$. The heat
comparison \eqref{eq:heat-comparison}, together with factorization
of the lattice heat kernel, gives
$$
 u(T,j,y)\geq\eta_0\mathsf p_1(T,j-j_0)\mathsf p_n(T,y-y_0).
$$
Let $a_{\max}=\max a_\perp$. Comparing the transverse linear equation
with the constant-potential equation yields
$$
 K_\perp(T;y,y_0)\leq\mathrm e^{a_{\max}T}\mathsf p_n(T,y-y_0).
$$
Choose $0<\varepsilon\leq a/K$ so small that
$$
 \varepsilon\beta_\perp T^{n/2}\mathrm e^{(a_{\max}-a)T}
          \leq\eta_0\mathsf p_1(T,0).
$$
At $j=j_0$ this restriction gives
$q(0,j_0)H_T(0,y;y_0)\leq u(T,j_0,y)$; at other longitudinal
sites $q(0,j)=0$. The initial ordering therefore holds everywhere.
Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed-domain-comparison}, applied to the subsolution
in \eqref{eq:product-subsolution-residual}, proves
\eqref{eq:product-comparison}. The two endpoints of $K_\perp$ are
retained throughout, since its value can depend on their individual
cell residues.

label: lem:logconcavity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:logconcavity}
The tilted kernel $G(t,j)$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:longitudinal} is
strictly positive and log-concave as a sequence in $j$ for every $t>0$:
$$
    G(t,j)^2\geq G(t,j-1)G(t,j+1)\qquad(j\in\mathbb Z).
$$
Consequently, $G(t,j+1)/G(t,j-1)$ is nonincreasing in $j$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use preservation of log-concavity under convolution and verify it
for the sequences in this argument. A nonnegative
summable sequence $a$ with interval support and
$a_k^2\geq a_{k-1}a_{k+1}$ has a Toeplitz matrix
$T(a)_{ij}=a_{i-j}$ whose $2\times2$ minors are nonnegative. Indeed,
for $i<j$ and $r<s$, the two indices in
$a_{i-r}a_{j-s}$ lie between the two indices in
$a_{i-s}a_{j-r}$, and their sums are equal. The monotonicity of
successive ratios on the positive support gives
$$
    a_{i-r}a_{j-s}\geq a_{i-s}a_{j-r}.
$$
If the right-hand product is positive, interval support justifies all
successive ratios between its two indices and the displayed inequality follows
from their monotonicity. If the right-hand product is zero, the inequality follows directly
from nonnegativity.

If both $a$ and $b$ have this property, the finite Cauchy--Binet formula
shows that every $2\times2$ minor of
$T(a)_{\{i,j\},[-N,N]}T(b)_{[-N,N],\{r,s\}}$ is nonnegative.
Its entries converge to those of $T(a*b)_{\{i,j\},\{r,s\}}$ as
$N\to\infty$, since the convolution sums converge absolutely.
Thus $a*b$ is log-concave as well.

The distribution of a Poisson random variable has interval support and
successive ratio $\rho/(k+1)$ on its positive support, where $\rho>0$
is its parameter. It is therefore log-concave. Reflection preserves
log-concavity. The kernel $G(t,\cdot)$ is the convolution of the
Poisson distribution with parameter $\mathrm e^{\lambda_*}t$ and the
reflected Poisson distribution with parameter $\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*}t$.
The convolution property proves the asserted inequality. Moreover,
$G(t,j)>0$ for every $j\in\mathbb Z$ because the two independent Poisson variables
can realize, for example, the pair $(j,0)$ when $j\ge0$ and $(0,-j)$ when
$j<0$. Its successive ratios are
positive and nonincreasing, so the product of two adjacent ratios,
$G(t,j+1)/G(t,j-1)$, is nonincreasing.
head: environment

label: lem:autonomous-leading-lower
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:positive-part-inequality
title: Proof
body_md:
Take $g=\1_{\{1\}}-\1_{\{-1\}}$ and put
$$
    w(t,j)=G(t,j-1)-G(t,j+1),\qquad
    Z(t,j)=\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*(j-c_*t)}w(t,j),
    \qquad W=Z_+.
$$
By critical conjugation, $Z$ solves $Z_t=\Delta_{\mathbb Z}Z+aZ$ with
initial datum
$\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*}\1_{\{1\}}-\mathrm e^{\lambda_*}\1_{\{-1\}}$.
The positive part satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positive-part-inequality}
    W_t\leq\Delta_{\mathbb Z}W+aW,
\end{equation}
for almost every time at each site. To check this, at a site where $Z>0$
the derivative is unchanged and replacing the neighboring values by their
positive parts can only increase the Laplacian. Where $Z<0$, the left
side is zero and the neighboring positive parts are nonnegative. The
derivative is zero almost everywhere on the time set where $Z=0$.
Countability of the lattice gives a common exceptional null set.

We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:integrable-positive-mode}
    \sup_{j\in\mathbb Z}W(t,j)\leq C_0(1+t)^{-3/2}\qquad(t\geq0),
\end{equation}
for a constant $C_0$. Let $j_{\rm cut}(t)=\lfloor c_*t\rfloor-2$.
Then $-3\leq j_{\rm cut}(t)-c_*t\leq-2$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:longitudinal}, together with $0<\delta_*<1/2$, shows
that $w(t,j_{\rm cut}(t))<0$ for every sufficiently large $t$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:logconcavity} now implies $w(t,j)\leq0$ for
$j\leq j_{\rm cut}(t)$: the ratio $G(t,j+1)/G(t,j-1)$ is at least
its value at $j_{\rm cut}(t)$, which exceeds
one. Therefore $W(t,j)>0$ is possible only when $j-c_*t\geq-3$.
For $-3\leq s:=j-c_*t\leq\sqrt t$, the expansion
\eqref{eq:signed-kernel} in Lemma~\ref{lem:longitudinal}, used with a fixed
diffusive constant, gives
$$
    W(t,j)\leq Ct^{-3/2}(1+|s|)\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*s}
             \leq C't^{-3/2}.
$$
For $s>\sqrt t$, use $|w(t,j)|\leq2$ to obtain
$W(t,j)\leq2\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*\sqrt t}\leq C't^{-3/2}$.
On any remaining bounded time interval, the heat representation for
$Z$ gives
$\lVert Z(t,\cdot)\rVert_\infty\leq
 \mathrm e^{at}(\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*}+\mathrm e^{\lambda_*})$.
Increasing $C_0$ proves \eqref{eq:integrable-positive-mode}.

Choose a site $j_0$ with $Q(0,j_0)>0$ and let
$\widetilde W(t,j)=W(t,j-j_0+1)$. Define
$$
    \chi(t)=\left(\chi_0^{-1}
                 +KC_0\int_0^t(1+s)^{-3/2}\mathrm d s\right)^{-1},
$$
where $\chi_0>0$ is chosen so that
$\chi_0\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*}\leq Q(0,j_0)$ and
$\chi_0C_0\leq a/K$. Then
$$
    0<(\chi_0^{-1}+2KC_0)^{-1}\leq\chi(t)\leq\chi_0.
$$
Using \eqref{eq:positive-part-inequality} and
\eqref{eq:integrable-positive-mode}, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
    &(\partial_t-\Delta_{\mathbb Z})(\chi\widetilde W)
               -a\chi\widetilde W+K\chi^2\widetilde W^2\\
    &\qquad\leq
       \chi^2\widetilde W\bigl[-KC_0(1+t)^{-3/2}
                                      +K\widetilde W\bigr]\leq0.
\end{aligned}
$$
The initial positive part is supported only at $j_0$, and the choice
of $\chi_0$ gives $\chi(0)\widetilde W(0,j)\leq Q(0,j)$ at every
site. The residual above and Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed-domain-comparison}
therefore give $Q\geq\chi\widetilde W$.

Finally, fix $A>0$ and choose $L_0$ so large that, for
$L_0\leq s=j-c_*t\leq A\sqrt t$, one has
$s/2\leq s-j_0+1\leq(A+1)\sqrt t$ for all sufficiently large $t$.
Use Lemma~\ref{lem:longitudinal} on this fixed diffusive window.
The Gaussian factor there has a positive lower bound depending on $A$,
whereas the remainder divided by the positive leading term tends to
zero uniformly. After the inverse exponential weight, the fixed spatial
translation changes only a constant factor. The positive lower bound
for $\chi$ proves \eqref{eq:autonomous-leading-lower}.

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\sigma_\mu=2(\cosh(\lambda_*+\mu)-1)+a
                   -c_*(\lambda_*+\mu)$.
The function
$k\mapsto2(\cosh k-1)+a-c_*k$ is strictly convex. It and its first
derivative vanish at $k=\lambda_*$, so $\sigma_\mu>0$.
Moreover, $\omega_\mu\mu<1/2$ and
$$
    \frac r2\leq P_\mu(r)\leq r,\qquad
    \frac12<P_\mu'(r)\leq1\qquad(r\geq0).
$$
On $[-1,0]$, convexity of $P_\mu$ and the values
$P_\mu(-1)=-1/2$, $P_\mu(0)=0$ give $P_\mu\leq0$.
Thus truncating the profile to zero on $r\leq0$ improves the
Laplacian inequality at the left edge.

Temporarily define
$F_\varepsilon(r)=\varepsilon\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}P_\mu(r)$
on the whole real line. For a function of a real argument, write
$\Delta_1F(r)=F(r-1)-2F(r)+F(r+1)$.
The critical identities \eqref{eq:critical-system} give the exact
calculation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pulse-linear-residual}
    -c_*F_\varepsilon'(r)-\Delta_1F_\varepsilon(r)
                        -aF_\varepsilon(r)
       =-\varepsilon\omega_\mu\sigma_\mu
                                     \mathrm e^{-(\lambda_*+\mu)r}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the operator on the left annihilates both
$\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}$ and $r\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}$; applying it to
$\varepsilon\omega_\mu\mathrm e^{-(\lambda_*+\mu)r}$ gives exactly the
right-hand side of \eqref{eq:pulse-linear-residual}.

For $r>0$, the only possible difference between
$\Delta_1\Phi_\varepsilon(r)$ and $\Delta_1F_\varepsilon(r)$
is the value at $r-1$ when $0<r<1$. That value of
$F_\varepsilon$ is nonpositive, while its truncated value is zero.
Consequently
$\Delta_1\Phi_\varepsilon(r)\geq\Delta_1F_\varepsilon(r)$.
Set $M_\mu:=\sup_{r\geq0}r^2\mathrm e^{-(\lambda_*-\mu)r}
=4/(\mathrm e^2(\lambda_*-\mu)^2)$. Choose
$$
    0<\varepsilon_*\leq
      \min\left\{\frac{a\mathrm e\lambda_*}{K},
                  \frac{\omega_\mu\sigma_\mu}{2KM_\mu}\right\}.
$$
The first restriction gives $\Phi_\varepsilon\leq a/K$, and the
second, together with $P_\mu(r)\leq r$, implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pulse-nonlinear-residual}
    -c_*\Phi_\varepsilon'(r)-\Delta_1\Phi_\varepsilon(r)
                     -a\Phi_\varepsilon(r)+K\Phi_\varepsilon(r)^2
       \leq-\frac{\varepsilon\omega_\mu\sigma_\mu}{2}
                                  \mathrm e^{-(\lambda_*+\mu)r}
       \qquad(r>0).
\end{equation}

Put $\tau=t+T$. The extra terms produced by the moving argument and
the time-dependent growth rate are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pulse-temporal-residual}
\begin{split}
    \frac1\tau\bigl(b_\beta\Phi_\varepsilon'(r)
                                      +\beta\Phi_\varepsilon(r)\bigr)
      &=\frac{\varepsilon\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}}\tau
          \left[b_\beta P_\mu'(r)-\frac32P_\mu(r)\right]\\
      &\leq\frac{\varepsilon\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}}\tau
                       \left(b_\beta-\frac34r\right).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
For $r\geq R_0:=1+4b_\beta/3$, this quantity is nonpositive.
For $0<r<R_0$, it is at most
$\varepsilon b_\beta\tau^{-1}\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}$, which is
absorbed by \eqref{eq:pulse-nonlinear-residual} once
$$
    \tau\geq\tau_*:=
       \max\left\{1,
          \frac{2b_\beta\mathrm e^{\mu R_0}}{\omega_\mu\sigma_\mu}\right\}.
$$
For $r<0$, the pulse value and its time derivative are zero, while
neighboring values are nonnegative. Its residual is therefore
$-\Delta_{\mathbb Z}\Psi\leq0$. The profile $\Phi_\varepsilon$ is globally
Lipschitz and smooth away from zero, so its value at each lattice site
is locally absolutely continuous in time. The argument
$j-c_*t+b_\beta\log(t+T)$ has only isolated zeros; these times do
not affect the almost-everywhere inequality. Combining
\eqref{eq:pulse-nonlinear-residual} and
\eqref{eq:pulse-temporal-residual} proves
\eqref{eq:delayed-pulse-subsolution}.

label: eq:nonautonomous-leading-lower
title: Proof
body_md:
Comparison with the constants $0$ and $a/K$ gives
$0\leq q\leq a/K$: at the latter constant, the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:scalar-growth-loss} equals
$-a\beta/[K(t+T)]\leq0$. This bound also extends the solution to
all positive times.
Since $aq-Kq^2\geq0$ on this interval,
$q(t,j)\geq\mathrm e^{-\beta t/T}(\mathrm e^{t\Delta_{\mathbb Z}}q_0)(j)>0$ for $t>0$.
Let $Q$ be the autonomous logistic solution with initial datum $q_0$,
and put $\rho(t)=(T/(t+T))^\beta$. Direct substitution gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
    &(\partial_t-\Delta_{\mathbb Z})(\rho Q)
         -\left(a-\frac\beta{t+T}\right)\rho Q+K\rho^2Q^2\\
    &\hspace{4em}=-K\rho(1-\rho)Q^2\leq0.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $\rho(0)=1$, comparison gives $q\geq\rho Q$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:autonomous-leading-lower}, applied with $A=2\sigma+1$,
consequently gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonautonomous-leading-lower}
    q(t,j)\geq c_0T^\beta(t+T)^{-\beta}t^{-3/2}
                     (j-c_*t)\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*(j-c_*t)},
\end{equation}
for large $t$ and $L_0\leq j-c_*t\leq(2\sigma+1)\sqrt t$.

Write $\tau=t+T$ and set
$B(t):=c_*t-b_\beta\log\tau+\sigma\sqrt\tau$.
This right endpoint is strictly increasing for large $t$.
At a collar vertex $B(t)<j\leq B(t)+1$, one has
$\sigma\sqrt\tau<r:=r(t,j)\leq\sigma\sqrt\tau+1$ and
$s:=j-c_*t=r-b_\beta\log\tau$.
For all sufficiently large $t$, uniformly over this collar,
$$
    L_0\leq s\leq(2\sigma+1)\sqrt t,\qquad s\geq r/2.
$$
Since $\lambda_*b_\beta=\beta+3/2$, estimate
\eqref{eq:nonautonomous-leading-lower} becomes
$$
\begin{aligned}
    q(t,j)
      &\geq c_0T^\beta\left(\frac\tau t\right)^{3/2}
                                  s\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}\\
      &\geq c_1r\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r},
       \qquad c_1:=c_0T^\beta/2>0.
\end{aligned}
$$
On the other hand,
$\Phi_\varepsilon(r)\leq\varepsilon r\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}$.
Thus the full right-collar ordering holds if $\varepsilon\leq c_1$.

Choose $t_0$ large enough for this collar estimate, the monotonicity of
$B$, the inequality $t_0+T\geq\tau_*$ in
Lemma~\ref{lem:delayed-pulse}, and $\sigma\sqrt{t_0+T}\geq2$.
The constants $c_1$ and $t_0$ may depend on the equation, $q_0$, $\mu$
and $\sigma$, but not on the amplitude subsequently chosen in
$(0,\varepsilon_*]$.
At time $t_0$, only finitely many interior sites have
$0<r(t_0,j)\leq\sigma\sqrt{t_0+T}$, and $q(t_0,j)>0$ at each
one. We may therefore choose
$0<\varepsilon\leq\min\{\varepsilon_*,c_1\}$ still smaller so that
$$
    \Phi_\varepsilon(r(t_0,j))\leq q(t_0,j)
                 \qquad(j\leq B(t_0)).
$$
The remaining interior sites satisfy the initial ordering because
$\Phi_\varepsilon(r)=0$ for $r\leq0$.

Lemma~\ref{lem:delayed-pulse} supplies the differential inequality on
the whole lattice. The right-collar estimate and the initial ordering
therefore permit the use of Lemma~\ref{lem:moving-halfline-comparison}
on $[t_0,t_1]$ for every finite $t_1>t_0$. This proves
\eqref{eq:scalar-profile-lower} for all $t\geq t_0$, including the
integer-crossing times of the moving endpoint.
At the integer in \eqref{eq:scalar-positive-seed}, $1\leq r<2$.
The positive minimum
$\eta:=\min_{1\leq r\leq2}\Phi_\varepsilon(r)$ therefore proves the
last assertion.

label: lem:amplification
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:amplification}
Under \eqref{eq:periodic-kpp}, for each $\eta,\theta\in(0,1)$ there
is $S>0$ such that any $[0,1]$-valued solution with
$u(t_0,z)\geq\eta$ satisfies
$u(t_0+s,z)\geq\theta$ for every $s\geq S$.
The constant is uniform in $z$, $t_0$ and the solution.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Q_L=\{-L,\ldots,L\}^d$ and define
$$
 \varphi_L(x)=\prod_{i=1}^d\cos\frac{\pi x_i}{2L+2}
 \quad(x\in Q_L),\qquad \varphi_L=0\quad\text{outside }Q_L.
$$
On $Q_L$ this function satisfies
$-\Delta\varphi_L=\mu_L\varphi_L$, where
$\mu_L=2d(1-\cos(\pi/(2L+2)))\to0$.
Choose $L$ with $\mu_L<\min_{x\in\mathcal C}a(x)$.
The finite-cell limit $F(x,s)/s\to a(x)$ as $s\downarrow0$
then gives $\varepsilon_L>0$ such that
$F(x,s)>\mu_Ls$ for every lattice site and
$0<s\leq\varepsilon_L$. Thus
$\varepsilon\varphi_L$ is a strict stationary subsolution of the
Dirichlet problem on $Q_L$ whenever
$0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_L$. The value one inside the box,
with zero exterior values, is a supersolution on $Q_L$.
Comparison and the order-preserving flow show that the Dirichlet
solution starting from $\varepsilon\varphi_L$ increases and remains
below one. It therefore converges to a positive equilibrium $q_L$.
The limit is stationary: continuity of the finite-dimensional vector
field makes each component derivative converge, and a nonzero
limiting derivative would contradict convergence of that component.

We show that every such choice of positive box equilibria converges
locally to one as $L\to\infty$. Fix $K_0$ with
$\mu_{K_0}<\min a$, and choose $b\in(0,1)$ such that
$F(x,s)>\mu_{K_0}s$ uniformly in $x$ for $0<s\leq b$.
For each translated box $z+Q_{K_0}\subset Q_L$, increase
$\sigma\varphi_{K_0}(\cdot-z)$ from zero while keeping it below
$q_L$. A first contact at $0<\sigma<b$ would occur inside the
smaller box and give
$$
 0\leq\Delta(q_L-\sigma\varphi_{K_0}(\cdot-z))(x)
 =\mu_{K_0}\sigma\varphi_{K_0}(x-z)
       -F(x,\sigma\varphi_{K_0}(x-z))<0.
$$
The first inequality follows because the difference is zero at the
contact site and nonnegative at all its neighbors, including those
outside the smaller box. Consequently the profile can be increased
to $\sigma=b$, and $q_L(z)\geq b$ whenever
$z+Q_{K_0}\subset Q_L$. This bound depends only on the fixed small
box and the reaction, not on the initial amplitude or the choice of
positive box equilibrium.

Any diagonal subsequential limit on the full lattice now satisfies
$b\leq q\leq1$ and $\Delta q+F(x,q)=0$.
Let $m=\inf q$ and choose $x_k$ with $q(x_k)\to m$. Then
$$
 -F(x_k,q(x_k))=\Delta q(x_k)
       \geq-2d(q(x_k)-m).
$$
Along a fixed-residue subsequence, the left-hand reaction tends to
$-F(r_0,m)$. Since $m\geq b>0$ and $F(r_0,m)>0$ for $m<1$,
the inequality forces $m=1$ and hence $q\equiv1$.
A failure of local convergence to one would produce a diagonal
limit below one at some fixed site, contradicting this conclusion.
The same argument applies to every translate of the reaction, and
there are only $|\mathcal C|$ such phases.

Start the full equation from $\eta\1_{\{z\}}$.
At time one its value at $x$ is at least
$\eta\mathsf p_d(1,x-z)>0$. Choose one sufficiently large box size
for all reaction phases so that every positive box equilibrium
obtained above has center value greater than $\theta$.
Inside the box centered at $z$, choose
$\varepsilon>0$ with
$\varepsilon\varphi_L(\cdot-z)\leq
\eta\mathsf p_d(1,\cdot-z)$ and $\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_L$.
The amplitude can also be chosen uniformly over the finitely many
phases. The corresponding increasing Dirichlet solution lies below the
full solution and eventually exceeds $\theta$ at its center;
monotonicity keeps it above $\theta$ thereafter. For each of the
finitely many reaction phases this takes a finite time. Their
maximum, including the initial unit time, gives a common $S$.

Finally, if another solution satisfies $u(t_0,z)\geq\eta$, its
state at $t_0$ lies above $\eta\1_{\{z\}}$. The comparison principle
therefore gives $u(t_0+s,z)\geq\theta$ for every $s\geq S$.
The argument uses only the state at $t_0$, so it also applies to
an entire solution restarted at any finite time.

title: Proof
body_md:
Factorization \eqref{eq:transverse-factorization} and the evenness
of $H_\perp$ give
$\nabla H(\lambda_*e_1)=c_*e_1$ and
$H(\lambda_*e_1)=c_*\lambda_*$. Thus
$p_{e_1}=\lambda_*e_1$ and $w(e_1)=c_*$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:upper} gives the positive-axis upper bound
$\sup\{j:u(t,j,y)\geq\theta\}\leq m_d(t)+C_\theta$,
uniformly for $y\in\mathbb Z^{d-1}$. Its application to $-e_1$
gives the negative-axis upper bound. The critical exponent here is
determined by the transverse principal eigenvalue
$a_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

For the lower bound, use Lemma~\ref{lem:product-subsolution} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-logarithmic-lower} with
$\beta=(d-1)/2$, $\sigma=1$ and the chosen $K$. Then
$b_\beta=(d+2)/(2\lambda_*)$.
In the original time variable $s=T+t$, define
$$
 j_{\rm seed}(s)=\left\lceil m_d(s)-c_*T+1\right\rceil.
$$
The scalar pulse argument at this site is
$j_{\rm seed}(s)-m_d(s)+c_*T\in[1,2)$, so
$q(s-T,j_{\rm seed}(s))\geq\eta>0$ for all large $s$.
For each finite $A$, the local kernel estimate
\eqref{eq:transverse-kernel-local}, the positive minimum of
$\psi_\perp$ and the fixed value of $y_0$ give $h_A>0$ with
$$
 H_T(s-T,y;y_0)\geq h_A\qquad(|y|\leq A\sqrt s),
$$
for all sufficiently large $s$. The product comparison therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:section-seed}
 \inf_{|y|\leq A\sqrt s}u(s,j_{\rm seed}(s),y)\geq\eta_A>0.
\end{equation}

First take $A=0$ and choose the amplification time $S$ for the
axis seed level and the target $\theta$. For large $s$, the
function $a_0(s)=m_d(s)-c_*T+1$ is strictly increasing and tends
to infinity. Every sufficiently large integer $j$ is therefore
reached at a time $s_j$ with $a_0(s_j)=j$, and then
$j_{\rm seed}(s_j)=j$. The seed estimate and
Lemma~\ref{lem:amplification} give
$u(t,j,0)\geq\theta$ for every $t\geq s_j+S$.
Consequently the same bound holds at every sufficiently large
integer $j\leq a_0(t-S)$. Since
$$
 m_d(t)-m_d(t-S)
 =c_*S-\frac{d+2}{2\lambda_*}\log\frac{t}{t-S}
 \leq c_*S,
$$
a fixed $C_\theta$ ensures that this range contains every sufficiently
large integer below $m_d(t)-C_\theta$.
The remaining nonnegative integers form a finite set. At one fixed
positive time, \eqref{eq:heat-comparison} gives a positive minimum
of $u$ on that set, and a further application of
Lemma~\ref{lem:amplification} raises all its values to $\theta$
after one common time. This proves the inner axial interval.
Taking the integer part of its right endpoint gives the lower level
position, and hence \eqref{eq:axial-position}.

For \eqref{eq:diffusive-section}, apply \eqref{eq:section-seed}
with $2A+1$ in place of $A$, and let $S_A$ be the associated
amplification time. At $s=t-S_A$, every site with
$|y|\leq A\sqrt t$ belongs to the seed section for large $t$.
The uniformity of the amplification lemma in the lattice site gives
$$
 u(t,j_{\rm seed}(t-S_A),y)\geq\theta
       \qquad(|y|\leq A\sqrt t).
$$
The integer $j_{\rm seed}(t-S_A)$ differs from $m_d(t)$ by a bounded
amount, as required.

For \eqref{eq:axial-leading-edge}, fix $A\geq0$ and $\sigma>0$, and
apply Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-logarithmic-lower} with width
$\sigma+1$. In original time $s=T+t$, its argument is
$$
 r=j-m_d(s)+c_*T=\xi+c_*T.
$$
When $1\leq\xi\leq\sigma\sqrt s$, we have
$0<r\leq(\sigma+1)\sqrt s$ for large $s$. Since
$P_\mu(r)\geq r/2\geq(1+\xi)/4$, the product lower comparison gives
$$
 u(s,j,y)\geq
 \frac{\varepsilon h_A\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*c_*T}}4
       (1+\xi)\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*\xi}
       \qquad(|y|\leq A\sqrt s).
$$
For the upper bound, $p_{e_1}=\lambda_*e_1$ and
$H(p_{e_1})=c_*\lambda_*$ imply
$z_{e_1}(s,j,y)=\lambda_*\xi$. Substitution into
\eqref{eq:upper-main} gives
$u(s,j,y)\leq C(1+\lambda_*\xi)\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*\xi}$,
which has the required form after changing the constant.
Both constants are independent of the sites in the specified window.

For the negative axis, set $\widetilde j=-j$ and
$\widetilde F((\widetilde j,y),s)=F((-\widetilde j,y),s)$.
Its linearization is still $a_\perp(y)$, and the constants
$K_F$, $a_{\mathrm{eff}}$, $\lambda_*$ and $c_*$, as well as the
transverse kernel estimates, are unchanged. Applying the positive-axis
argument to the reflected equation gives all negative-axis conclusions.
If the linear growth rate is independent of another coordinate $x_i$,
a permutation makes that coordinate the longitudinal one, and the
same proof applies with the corresponding transverse operator.
These transformations preserve the assumptions even when the nonlinear
reaction depends on the longitudinal coordinate.

label: rem:fixed-transverse-rear
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:fixed-transverse-rear}
The inner estimate also holds uniformly over every fixed finite set
of transverse sites. For each $B\geq0$ and $\theta\in(0,1)$,
there are $C$ and $T$ such that
$u(t,j,y)\geq\theta$ whenever
$t\geq T$, $0\leq j\leq m_d(t)-C$ and $|y|\leq B$.
Indeed, use \eqref{eq:section-seed} with $A=1$; for large seed
times every such transverse site lies in its diffusive section.
The integer-arrival argument in the preceding proof and the uniform
amplification time then cover all sufficiently large $j$.
For the finitely many remaining pairs $(j,y)$,
\eqref{eq:heat-comparison} supplies a positive minimum at time one,
and Lemma~\ref{lem:amplification} raises that minimum to $\theta$
after a single additional time.

label: lem:entire-comparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:entire-comparison}
Let $V,W$ be entire $[0,1]$-valued solutions for the same periodic
reaction. Choose $\delta,\nu>0$ such that
$F_s(x,s)\leq-\nu$ for $1-\delta\leq s\leq1$ and every $x$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $V\geq1-\delta$ on a set $E\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb Z^d$ and
$W\leq V$ on its complement, then $W\leq V$ everywhere.
\item If $W\leq V$ and equality holds at one space--time point,
then $W\equiv V$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $D=(W-V)_+$. Wherever $D>0$, the assumed ordering outside $E$
places both solution values in $[1-\delta,1]$. The reaction difference
is therefore at most $-\nu D$. The discrete positive-part inequality
gives, almost everywhere in time,
$$
 D_t\leq\Delta D-\nu D.
$$
At a site where $D=0$, this follows because the positive part has zero
derivative almost everywhere and $\Delta D\geq0$. Since $0\leq D\leq1$,
comparison from time $t-h$ yields
$D(t)\leq\mathrm e^{-\nu h}\mathrm e^{h\Delta}D(t-h)\leq\mathrm e^{-\nu h}$.
Letting $h\to\infty$ proves the first assertion.

For the second, the nonnegative difference $D=V-W$ satisfies
$D_t=\Delta D+b(t,x)D$ with $b$ uniformly bounded. If
$D(t_0,x_0)=0$ and $K\geq\|b\|_\infty$, comparison with the heat
equation gives, for every $h>0$,
$$
 0\geq\mathrm e^{-Kh}
 \sum_{y\in\mathbb Z^d}\mathsf p_d(h,x_0-y)D(t_0-h,y).
$$
Every summand is nonnegative and the heat kernel is strictly positive.
Thus $D$ vanishes at every time before $t_0$, and uniqueness for the
linear lattice equation gives the same conclusion afterwards.

We also need this zero-contact argument for the linear limits below,
which can grow exponentially in space. For $\rho>0$, define
$$
 X_\rho=\left\{f:\|f\|_\rho=
       \sup_{x\in\mathbb Z^d}\mathrm e^{-\rho|x|_1}|f(x)|<\infty\right\}.
$$
Neighbor shifts have norm at most $\mathrm e^\rho$ on $X_\rho$, so
$\|\Delta\|\leq2d(\mathrm e^\rho+1)$ there. Multiplication by bounded $b$
is also bounded. A solution bounded in this norm on compact time
intervals satisfies the integral equation in $X_\rho$, where Gronwall's
inequality gives uniqueness and the same heat comparison. The heat-kernel
sum converges because the Poisson jump count has finite exponential
moments. Consequently zero contact also forces equality in this class.

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $r=x\cdot n-ct$. The solution has a positive lower bound on every
strip $-A\leq r\leq A$. To see this, choose a fixed $h>0$ that moves
the earlier coordinate $r+ch$ into a compact interval in the positive
tail. The tail lower bound and $V_t\geq-2dV$ then give a uniform
positive lower bound at the current point.

Fix $\ell\in\Gamma$ and set
$W_\tau(t,x)=V(t+\tau,x+\ell)$ and
$\sigma(\tau)=n\cdot\ell-c\tau$.
Choose $A$ so that $V\geq1-\delta$ when $r<-A$, with $\delta$ as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:entire-comparison}. For large positive $\sigma$, the
lower bound for $V$ on each fixed strip and the tail upper bound for
$W_\tau$ give $W_\tau\leq V$ on that strip. Farther to the right,
the ratio of the upper bound for $W_\tau$ to the lower bound for $V$
is at most $C(1+\sigma)\mathrm e^{-\lambda\sigma}<1$. The comparison lemma
extends the ordering to $r<-A$. Hence $W_\tau\leq V$ for all
sufficiently negative $\tau$.

Let $\tau_*$ be the supremum of the times up to which the ordering
holds for every earlier shift. This value is finite, since at a fixed
point $W_\tau\to1>V$ as $\tau\to\infty$. Continuity in $\tau$ gives
$W_{\tau_*}\leq V$. We claim that
$\sigma_*=n\cdot\ell-c\tau_*\leq0$.
If $\sigma_*>0$, there are $\tau_k\downarrow\tau_*$ at which the
ordering fails. By Lemma~\ref{lem:entire-comparison}, we can choose
failure points $(t_k,x_k)$ with $r_k=x_k\cdot n-ct_k\geq-A$.
After a subsequence, $x_k\bmod\Gamma=r_0$ is fixed.

Suppose first that $r_k$ is bounded, and choose a subsequence with
$r_k\to r_\infty$. Translation compactness from
Section~\ref{sec:spectral} gives a local $C^1$ limit
$V_\infty(s,z)$ of $V(t_k+s,x_k+z)$. It solves the equation with
reaction $F(r_0+z,\cdot)$ and inherits the invaded-region limit and
the two-sided tail, with coordinate $r_\infty+n\cdot z-cs$.
The ordered difference
$V_\infty(s,z)-V_\infty(s+\tau_*,z+\ell)$ is nonnegative and
vanishes at $(0,0)$, so the comparison lemma makes it identically
zero. The limit lies strictly between zero and one: attaining either
endpoint would make it the corresponding constant solution by the
same lemma, contrary to its end-state bounds. Iteration now gives
$V_\infty(0,0)=V_\infty(m\tau_*,m\ell)$, whose right-hand side tends
to zero as $m\to\infty$ because the front coordinate increases by
$m\sigma_*$. This is a contradiction.

If instead $r_k\to\infty$, put
$A_k=(1+r_k)\mathrm e^{-\lambda r_k}$ and
$Z_k(s,z)=A_k^{-1}V(t_k+s,x_k+z)$.
On each compact time interval and finite set of sites, the tail bounds
give positive upper and lower bounds for $Z_k$. The equation also
bounds its first and second time derivatives there. Since $A_k\to0$,
Taylor's formula gives, for any local limit,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalized-linear-limit}
 Z_s=\Delta Z+a(r_0+z)Z,\qquad
 b\mathrm e^{-\lambda(n\cdot z-cs)}\leq Z(s,z)
                  \leq B\mathrm e^{-\lambda(n\cdot z-cs)}.
\end{equation}
The original constants $b,B$ remain valid because
$(1+r_k+n\cdot z-cs)/(1+r_k)\to1$.
The ordering at $\tau_*$ passes to the limit. The failed inequalities
at $\tau_k$, together with the local derivative bound for $Z_k$,
give equality at $(0,0)$. Thus
$Z(s,z)-Z(s+\tau_*,z+\ell)$ is a nonnegative solution of the same
linear equation with zero contact. Its growth satisfies the weighted
comparison class in Lemma~\ref{lem:entire-comparison}, so it vanishes
identically. Iterating this identity and using
\eqref{eq:normalized-linear-limit} yields
$0<Z(0,0)\leq B\mathrm e^{-m\lambda\sigma_*}$ for every $m$, again a
contradiction.

We have proved $\tau_*\geq n\cdot\ell/c$ and therefore
$V(t+n\cdot\ell/c,x+\ell)\leq V(t,x)$. Applying this result to
$-\ell$ and evaluating it at $(t+n\cdot\ell/c,x+\ell)$ gives the
reverse inequality. This proves \eqref{eq:covariance}.
With $\ell=0$, the same sliding argument gives
$V(t+\tau,x)\leq V(t,x)$ for every $\tau\leq0$, hence $V_t\geq0$.
The function $V_t$ satisfies a bounded-coefficient linear equation.
Zero contact would make it vanish identically. A time-independent
solution cannot satisfy both moving-region bounds in
\eqref{eq:rigidity-hyp} when $c>0$, so $V_t>0$.

Define $\Phi(s,x)=V((n\cdot x-s)/c,x)$. Periodic covariance makes
$\Phi$ $\Gamma$-periodic in $x$, and $V_t>0$ makes it strictly
decreasing in $s$. The assumed bounds give its uniform end states
$1,0$. Substitution into the lattice equation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pulsating-profile-equation}
 -c\Phi_s(s,x)=\sum_{|z|_1=1}
   \bigl(\Phi(s+n\cdot z,x+z)-\Phi(s,x)\bigr)+F(x,\Phi(s,x)),
\end{equation}
which completes the proof.

label: prop:profile-limits
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:profile-limits}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:axial}, let
$t_k\to\infty$ and $x_k=(j_k,y_k)$ satisfy
$|j_k-m_d(t_k)|\leq C$ and $|y_k|\leq A\sqrt{t_k}$ for fixed
$C,A\geq0$. After passage to a subsequence, $x_k\bmod\Gamma=r_0\in\mathcal C$ is
constant and $u(t_k+s,x_k+z)$ converges uniformly for $s$ in each compact
time interval and $z$ in each finite subset of $\mathbb Z^d$ to a critical
pulsating front for $F^{[r_0]}$. Its direction is $e_1$ and its speed is
$c_*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After a subsequence, let $x_k\bmod\Gamma=r_0$,
$j_k-m_d(t_k)\to\delta$, and $y_k/\sqrt{t_k}\to\eta$.
Translation compactness from Section~\ref{sec:spectral} gives a local
$C^1$ limit $V(s,z)$ of $u(t_k+s,x_k+z)$, satisfying
$V_s=\Delta_{\mathbb Z^d}V+F(r_0+z,V)$.
For $r=z_1-c_*s$, Theorem~\ref{thm:upper}, with
$p_{e_1}=\lambda_*e_1$, gives
$V(s,z)\leq B(1+r)\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*r}$ for all sufficiently large $r$.

The pointwise comparisons \eqref{eq:product-comparison} and
\eqref{eq:scalar-profile-lower} supply the matching lower tail.
At $(t_k+s,x_k+z)$, the pulse argument tends to
$r+\delta+c_*T$ and eventually lies below the diffusive cutoff in
Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-logarithmic-lower}, used with $\sigma=1$.
Writing $z=(z_1,z')$ and $r_0=(r_{0,1},r_{0,\perp})$, the transverse
factor converges by \eqref{eq:transverse-kernel-local} to
$$
 \frac{\beta_\perp|\mathcal C_\perp|
        \psi_\perp(r_{0,\perp}+z')\psi_\perp(y_0)}
      {(2\pi)^{(d-1)/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma_\perp}}
       \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\eta^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\perp^{-1}\eta\right).
$$
Its minimum over the transverse cell is a number $h_\eta>0$.
The diagonal limit therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:limit-pulse-bound}
 V(s,z)\geq h_\eta\Phi_\varepsilon(r+\delta+c_*T),
\end{equation}
for every $(s,z)$, with the same constant. This yields the required
positive critical lower tail. The two tail bounds exclude the constant
solutions zero and one; zero contact in
Lemma~\ref{lem:entire-comparison} then gives $0<V<1$ everywhere.

At a fixed site $z$, choose $s_0$ so that
$z_1-c_*s_0+\delta+c_*T=1$. Equation~\eqref{eq:limit-pulse-bound}
gives a positive seed at $(s_0,z)$ independent of $z$.
As $z_1-c_*s\to-\infty$, the elapsed time $s-s_0$ tends uniformly
to infinity. Lemma~\ref{lem:amplification} consequently gives the
uniform invaded-region limit $V\to1$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity} applies to the translated reaction and
identifies $V$ as a critical pulsating front. Translating one such
limit back by $r_0$ also gives a critical front for the original medium.

label: lem:tail-source
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The profile equation \eqref{eq:pulsating-profile-equation} and the
critical upper bound give
$|\Phi_s(s,x)|\leq C(1+s)\mathrm e^{-\lambda s}$ for $s\geq1$.
Differentiating the equation once gives the same bound for $\Phi_{ss}$,
since there are finitely many shifts and $F_s$ is bounded.
Both derivatives are also bounded on the whole cylinder: for the
associated entire solution,
$V_t=\Delta V+F(x,V)$ and
$V_{tt}=\Delta V_t+F_s(x,V)V_t$.

Set $N_x(r)=a(x)r-F(x,r)$. The KPP condition and Taylor's formula give
$0\leq N_x(r)\leq Cr^2$, $|N_x'(r)|\leq Cr$, and
$|N_x''(r)|\leq C$ on $[0,1]$, uniformly in the cell.
Thus
$$
 \begin{aligned}
 g_s&=\mathrm e^{\lambda s}
       \bigl(\lambda N_x(\Phi)+N_x'(\Phi)\Phi_s\bigr),\\
 g_{ss}&=\mathrm e^{\lambda s}\bigl(\lambda^2N_x(\Phi)
       +2\lambda N_x'(\Phi)\Phi_s
       +N_x''(\Phi)\Phi_s^2+N_x'(\Phi)\Phi_{ss}\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
$$
The profile bounds prove \eqref{eq:tail-source-derivatives} for $s\geq0$;
boundedness proves it for $s\leq0$. This uses only $C^2$ regularity of
$F$ in its second variable. Since $N_x(\Phi(s,x))\to a(x)>0$ as
$s\to-\infty$, the source is not zero.

The estimates give analyticity of $\widehat g$ by dominated
differentiation on smaller strips. Integrating by parts twice, with
vanishing boundary terms, gives
$z^2\widehat g(z)=\int\mathrm e^{-zs}g_{ss}(s)\,\mathrm d s$.
This proves \eqref{eq:tail-source-transform} for $|\tau|\geq1$;
the direct integral bound covers the remaining values.
Since $v=O(1+s)$ at $+\infty$ and $v=O(\mathrm e^{\lambda s})$ at
$-\infty$, its transform is analytic in the stated half-strip.

Multiplication of the profile equation by $\mathrm e^{\lambda s}$ gives
$$
 c v_s(s,x)+\sum_{|b|_1=1}\mathrm e^{-p\cdot b}v(s+n\cdot b,x+b)
       +(a(x)-2d-c\lambda)v(s,x)=g(s,x).
$$
Using $\widehat{v_s}(z)=z\widehat v(z)$ and
$\widehat{v(\cdot+\delta)}(z)=\mathrm e^{z\delta}\widehat v(z)$
proves \eqref{eq:tail-transform-equation}.

label: lem:critical-transform-gap
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The zero eigenvalue of $B_p-H(p)I$ is simple. Analytic perturbation
\cite[Chapter~II]{Kato} gives its spectral projection
$\phi_{p-zn}(\phi^*_{p-zn})^{\mathsf T}$, under the normalization
$(\phi^*_{p-zn})^{\mathsf T}\phi_{p-zn}=1$, and an analytic inverse on
the complementary subspace. This proves
\eqref{eq:critical-resolvent-local}.
The identities $H(p)=c\lambda$ and $n\cdot\nabla H(p)=c$ cancel
the constant and linear terms in $k$. Since its quadratic coefficient
is $D_n>0$, zero is the only singularity in a small disk.

To exclude other singularities on the imaginary axis, suppose
$\mathcal M(\mathrm i\tau)\xi=0$ with $\xi\ne0$, and write
$\xi(x)=\phi_p(x)\eta(x)$. Conjugation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:imaginary-axis-equation}
 \sum_{|z|_1=1}q_p(x,z)
      \bigl(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\tau n\cdot z}\eta(x+z)-\eta(x)\bigr)
                +\mathrm i c\tau\eta(x)=0.
\end{equation}
At a vertex of maximal nonzero $|\eta|$, multiply by its conjugate
and take real parts. Every jump term is nonpositive and their sum
is zero. Positivity of each rate therefore gives
$\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\tau n\cdot z}\eta(x+z)=\eta(x)$ on every outgoing edge.
Irreducibility propagates the maximal modulus and these identities
through the cell, including edges with identical endpoint residues.
The jump sum in \eqref{eq:imaginary-axis-equation} consequently
vanishes everywhere, so
$c\tau\eta=0$. Hence $\tau=0$.

For $|\operatorname{Re}z|\leq1$, the matrix
$B_{p-zn}-c\lambda I$ is uniformly bounded, because its oscillatory
factors have modulus one. Thus $\mathcal M(z)=czI+O(1)$ as
$|\operatorname{Im}z|\to\infty$, and a Neumann series proves
\eqref{eq:critical-resolvent-large}. The local expansion excludes
singularities near zero and this bound excludes them at large imaginary
part. On the remaining compact part of the imaginary axis,
$\det\mathcal M$ is nonzero. Continuity permits widening it to a
sufficiently small strip, proving the lemma for every direction $n$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:critical-tail-expansion}
Every profile in Theorem~\ref{thm:critical-uniqueness} satisfies
\eqref{eq:critical-tail-expansion} and \eqref{eq:critical-amplitude}.
In particular, its upper critical bound implies a positive two-sided
