label: eq:tail-inversion
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $0<\delta<\delta_0$. On $\operatorname{Re}z=\delta$,
\eqref{eq:tail-transform-equation} gives
$\widehat v(z)=\mathcal M(z)^{-1}\widehat g(z)$.
Lemmas~\ref{lem:tail-source} and~\ref{lem:critical-transform-gap}
bound the right-hand side by $C(1+|\operatorname{Im}z|)^{-3}$,
also on the line $\operatorname{Re}z=-\delta$.
For clarity, the inversion can be justified directly.
The function $f_\delta(s)=\mathrm e^{-\delta s}v(s)$ is continuous and
integrable, and its Fourier transform is integrable. Multiplying that
transform by $\mathrm e^{-\epsilon\tau^2}$ and applying Fubini's theorem
gives the convolution of $f_\delta$ with
$(4\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{-s^2/(4\epsilon)}$.
As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, the convolution converges pointwise to
$f_\delta$, while dominated convergence applies to the inverse integral.
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-inversion}
 v(s)=\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm i}
       \int_{\delta-\mathrm i\infty}^{\delta+\mathrm i\infty}
       \mathrm e^{zs}\mathcal M(z)^{-1}\widehat g(z)\,\mathrm d z.
\end{equation}

Move this contour to $\operatorname{Re}z=-\delta$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:critical-transform-gap} leaves only the pole at zero.
On the horizontal sides $z=\sigma\pm\mathrm i R$, $|\sigma|\leq\delta$,
the same two lemmas bound the integrand without $\mathrm e^{zs}$ by
$CR^{-3}$. For each fixed $s$, the horizontal integrals therefore
vanish as $R\to\infty$. The residue theorem gives
$$
 v(s)=\operatorname*{Res}_{z=0}
       \bigl(\mathrm e^{zs}\mathcal M(z)^{-1}\widehat g(z)\bigr)
 +\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm i}
   \int_{-\delta-\mathrm i\infty}^{-\delta+\mathrm i\infty}
      \mathrm e^{zs}\mathcal M(z)^{-1}\widehat g(z)\,\mathrm d z.
$$
Absolute integrability on the new line bounds the last term by
$C\mathrm e^{-\delta s}$ for $s\geq0$.

Set $\gamma(z)=(\phi^*_{p-zn})^{\mathsf T}\widehat g(z)$.
The singular part is $\phi_{p-zn}\gamma(z)/k(z)$.
The normalized eigenvectors and the spectral relation give
$$
 \phi_{p-zn}=\phi_p-z\dot\phi_p+O(z^2),\qquad
 k(z)=D_nz^2-\tfrac16H_n'''z^3+O(z^4),
$$
where $H_n'''=\left.\partial_\eta^3H(\eta n)\right|_{\eta=\lambda}$.
Consequently, with
$B_\Phi=\gamma'(0)/D_n+H_n'''\gamma(0)/(6D_n^2)$,
\begin{equation*}                             
 \mathcal M(z)^{-1}\widehat g(z)
  =\frac{A_\Phi\phi_p}{z^2}
      +\frac{B_\Phi\phi_p-A_\Phi\dot\phi_p}{z}+O(1),\qquad
 A_\Phi=\frac{\gamma(0)}{D_n}.
\end{equation*}
The coefficients are real on the real axis, so $B_\Phi\in\mathbb R$.
After multiplication by $\mathrm e^{zs}$, the residue in
\eqref{eq:tail-inversion} is
$(A_\Phi s+B_\Phi)\phi_p-A_\Phi\dot\phi_p$.
The integral for $\gamma(0)$ gives \eqref{eq:critical-amplitude}.
Its integrand is nonnegative and is positive for sufficiently negative
$s$, and $\phi_p^*>0$, so $A_\Phi>0$.
Dividing the contour formula by $\mathrm e^{\lambda s}$ proves
\eqref{eq:critical-tail-expansion}, uniformly over the finite cell.
The positivity of $A_\Phi$ and $\phi_p$ supplies the lower tail.

title: Proof
body_md:
The preceding lemma proves the expansion and the amplitude identity.
Its two-sided tail allows application of Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity}
to the entire solution associated with each profile. Thus each profile
is strictly decreasing in its first variable.

For two profiles $\Phi,\Psi$, put
\begin{equation*}                                         
 h_0=\frac1\lambda\log\frac{A_\Psi}{A_\Phi}.
\end{equation*}
Their expansions imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-profile-ratio}
 \frac{\Psi(s+h,x)}{\Phi(s,x)}
       \longrightarrow\frac{A_\Psi}{A_\Phi}\mathrm e^{-\lambda h}
       \qquad(s\to+\infty),
\end{equation}
uniformly in the cell and for $h$ in compact intervals.
We show that the shift $h_0$ matches the whole profiles.

For sufficiently large positive $h$, one has
$\Psi(s+h,x)\leq\Phi(s,x)$ for all $s,x$.
Choose $R$ so that $\Phi\geq1-\delta$ on $s<-R$.
On every fixed strip to its right, the positive minimum of $\Phi$
and the leading-edge limit of $\Psi$ give the ordering for large $h$.
For $s\geq R_1$ with a fixed sufficiently large $R_1$, the two-sided
tails give the uniform ratio bound $C(1+h)\mathrm e^{-\lambda h}<1$.
Writing the profiles as entire solutions, Lemma~\ref{lem:entire-comparison}
extends the ordering to $s<-R$.

Strict decrease of $\Psi$ makes the ordered shifts an upper interval.
Its lower endpoint $h_*$ is finite: the interval is nonempty, and
$\Psi(s+h,x)\to1>\Phi(s,x)$ at a fixed point as $h\to-\infty$.
Continuity gives $\Psi(s+h_*,x)\leq\Phi(s,x)$ everywhere, and
\eqref{eq:tail-profile-ratio} gives $h_*\geq h_0$.
If $h_*>h_0$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ with
$h_*-\varepsilon>h_0$. The uniform ratio limit gives a fixed strict
ordering for all $s\geq R_1$ and
$h\in[h_*-\varepsilon,h_*]$.
At $h_*$, contact in the compact strip $[-R,R_1]\times\mathcal C$
would make the entire solutions identical by
Lemma~\ref{lem:entire-comparison}; matching the tail amplitudes would
then give $h_*=h_0$. Thus the ordered difference has a positive minimum
on that strip. Decreasing $h$ slightly preserves the ordering there and
in the right tail, and the comparison lemma supplies it on $s<-R$.
This contradicts the definition of $h_*$. Hence $h_*=h_0$ and
$\Psi(\cdot+h_0,\cdot)\leq\Phi$.

Interchanging the profiles gives
$\Phi(\cdot-h_0,\cdot)\leq\Psi$. After changing the first variable,
this is the reverse inequality, so
$\Psi(s+h_0,x)=\Phi(s,x)$ everywhere.

label: rem:constant-linearization-tail
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:constant-linearization-tail}
Under \eqref{eq:common-linearization}, the normalized cell eigenvector
is $\phi_p\equiv|\mathcal C|^{-1}$ for every $p$, so $\dot\phi_p=0$.
In the axial direction, the expansion takes the simpler form
$$
 \Phi_*(s,x)=\mathrm e^{-\lambda_*s}
           \bigl(A_*s+B_*+O(\mathrm e^{-\delta s})\bigr),\qquad s\to+\infty,
$$
where $A_*>0$ and $B_*$ are independent of the cell variable.
Under \eqref{eq:transverse-linearization}, the axial eigenvector is
proportional to $\psi_\perp(y)$ and is still independent of $\lambda$.
Thus $\dot\phi_{\lambda e_1}=0$, while the first two tail terms carry
the transverse factor $\psi_\perp$.
In both cases the full profile may depend on the cell variable.
For a general periodic linearization, the additional term
$-A_\Phi\dot\phi_p(x)$ in \eqref{eq:critical-tail-expansion} is part
of the constant-order tail correction.

label: eq:phase-definition
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a limit from Proposition~\ref{prop:profile-limits} and translate
it back to the original medium. Its critical upper bound permits
application of Theorem~\ref{thm:critical-uniqueness}.
Strict decrease and the end states give a unique translate $\Phi_*$
with $\Phi_*(0,0)=1/2$, unique in the stated class.
Set $\ell(t)=\lfloor m_d(t)\rfloor$.
The values $u(t,\ell(t),0)$ stay in a compact subinterval of $(0,1)$
for large $t$: a sequence approaching an endpoint would have a profile
limit taking that endpoint at a finite point, contrary to the proposition.
We can therefore define a bounded phase by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase-definition}
 \zeta_0(t)=\bigl(\Phi_*(\cdot,(\ell(t),0))\bigr)^{-1}
                        (u(t,\ell(t),0))+m_d(t)-\ell(t).
\end{equation}
The inverses range over finitely many residues. Choose $T_1\geq2$
after which this definition is valid and extend $\zeta_0$ constantly
to $t<T_1$. This gives a bounded measurable function on $\mathbb R$.

We first prove the approximation with phase $\zeta_0$ on a fixed
window $|j-m_d(t)|\leq R$, $|y|\leq B$.
If it failed, there would be times $t_k\to\infty$ and sites in that
window with error bounded away from zero. Translate at the reference
sites $(\ell(t_k),0)$ and pass to a subsequence with fixed residue
$r_0$, fixed integer offset of the selected site, and
$\delta_k=m_d(t_k)-\ell(t_k)\to\delta$,
$\zeta_0(t_k)\to\zeta_\infty$.
Translation compactness and Proposition~\ref{prop:profile-limits},
followed by uniqueness, identify the local limit as
$\Phi_*(z_1-c_*s+\xi,z+r_0)$.
The reference-site identity \eqref{eq:phase-definition} implies
$\xi=\zeta_\infty-\delta$. At the selected offset, the first argument
of the approximating profile is
$z_1-\delta_k+\zeta_0(t_k)\to z_1+\xi$.
The approximation error consequently tends to zero, a contradiction.
To extend this convergence to $j\geq0$, use the right envelope in
Theorem~\ref{thm:upper} and the uniform left limit in
Remark~\ref{rem:fixed-transverse-rear}.
The end states of $\Phi_*$ are uniform in its finite cell and
$\zeta_0$ is bounded, so increasing $R$ proves the half-tube statement.

The phase changes slowly even when the reference integer $\ell(t)$
changes. Indeed, take $t_k\to\infty$ and $s_k\to s$ with
$|s_k|\leq S$. After a subsequence, the first reference residue and
$q=\ell(t_k+s_k)-\ell(t_k)$ are fixed. The local limit at that
reference site is a front with phase $\xi$ and speed $c_*$, while
$m_d(t_k+s_k)-m_d(t_k)\to c_*s$.
Writing $\delta_k'=m_d(t_k+s_k)-\ell(t_k+s_k)$ gives
$\delta_k'-\delta_k\to c_*s-q$.
At the second reference site, the inverse profile value in
\eqref{eq:phase-definition} tends to $q-c_*s+\xi$.
Its phase therefore tends to
$q-c_*s+\xi+\delta+c_*s-q=\xi+\delta$, the same limit as at the
first site. A subsequence contradiction now gives
$\sup_{|s|\leq S}|\zeta_0(t+s)-\zeta_0(t)|\to0$.

Choose $\varrho\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$, $\varrho\geq0$,
$\int\varrho=1$, and define
\begin{equation*}                               
 \zeta(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\varrho(s)\zeta_0(t-s)\,\mathrm d s.
\end{equation*}
Slow variation gives $\zeta(t)-\zeta_0(t)\to0$. Since
$\int\varrho'=0$,
$$
 |\zeta'(t)|\leq\|\varrho'\|_{L^1}
       \sup_{|s|\leq1}|\zeta_0(t-s)-\zeta_0(t)|\to0.
$$
The convolution is smooth and bounded. The profile equation bounds
$\partial_1\Phi_*$ globally, so replacement of $\zeta_0$ by $\zeta$
preserves \eqref{eq:profile-selection}.
This construction supplies slow phase variation; it does not require
the phase to converge to a constant.

Finally, set $P(t,j,y)=\Phi_*(j-m_d(t)+\zeta(t),(j,y))$.
At each fixed time, the profile equation gives
$\Delta P+F(x,P)=-c_*\partial_1\Phi_*(j-m_d(t)+\zeta(t),x)$.
For $j\geq1$, the approximation on $j\geq0$, $|y|\leq B+1$ and
the uniform Lipschitz bound for $F$ therefore give
\eqref{eq:profile-time-derivative}.
At $j=0$, there are finitely many sites for fixed $B$.
Positivity and Lemma~\ref{lem:amplification} give $u\to1$ at these
sites and their neighbors, hence $u_t\to0$ there.
The uniform invaded-region limit and the profile equation likewise give
$\partial_1\Phi_*(s,x)\to0$ as $s\to-\infty$.
Since $m_d(t)\to\infty$ and $\zeta$ is bounded, this handles the
remaining sites. Also $m_d'(t)\to c_*$ and $\zeta'(t)\to0$, so
$u_t-P_t\to0$ on each fixed-width half-tube.

label: cor:residue-limit
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:residue-limit}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:axial}, let $t_k\to\infty$
and $x_k=(j_k,y_k)$ satisfy $|j_k-m_d(t_k)|\leq C$ and
$|y_k|\leq A\sqrt{t_k}$ for fixed $C,A\geq0$. If
$x_k\bmod\Gamma=r_0$ and $u(t_k,x_k)\to\theta\in(0,1)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:residue-limit}
 u(t_k+s,x_k+z)\to
 \Phi_*(z_1-c_*s+\xi_{\theta,r_0},z+r_0),\qquad
 \Phi_*(\xi_{\theta,r_0},r_0)=\theta,
\end{equation}
uniformly for $s$ in compact intervals and $z$ in finite subsets of
$\mathbb Z^d$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:profile-limits} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:critical-uniqueness} make every entire subsequential limit a front
$\Phi_*(z_1-c_*s+\xi,z+r_0)$.
Its value at $(0,0)$ is $\theta$, so strict decrease fixes
$\xi=\xi_{\theta,r_0}$. All subsequences have the same limit, proving
\eqref{eq:residue-limit}.
If $j_k\geq0$, $y_k$ is bounded and
$u(t_k,j_k,y_k)\to\theta\in(0,1)$, the upper envelope excludes
$j_k\geq m_d(t_k)+C$, and the fixed-width rear estimate excludes
$j_k\leq m_d(t_k)-C$, for a sufficiently large fixed $C$.
Thus the required displacement bound holds automatically in this case.
At transverse distances of order $\sqrt{t_k}$, we use the displacement
bound stated in Proposition~\ref{prop:profile-limits}.

label: cor:arrival-times
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $0<\eta_-<\theta_-<\theta_+<\eta_+<1$.
For large $t$, if $\theta_-\leq u(t,j,y)\leq\theta_+$ in the
specified half-tube, the approximating profile lies in
$[\eta_-,\eta_+]$. The inverse profiles over the finite cell confine
its first argument to a compact interval $I$.
The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity} gives
$-c_*\partial_1\Phi_*>0$. Continuity and compactness therefore give
$\min_{I\times\mathcal C}(-c_*\partial_1\Phi_*)>0$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:profile-time-derivative} then proves
\eqref{eq:temporal-transversality}. The same argument with slightly
wider level bounds gives a positive derivative throughout a small
open neighborhood of $[\theta_-,\theta_+]$ for all sufficiently
large times.

For a fixed $t_0$, \eqref{eq:global-exponential-bound} gives, with any
$\lambda>0$,
$$
 \sup_{0\leq t\leq t_0,\ |y|\leq B}u(t,j,y)
 \leq C_\lambda\mathrm e^{c_\lambda t_0-\lambda j}\to0
 \qquad(j\to\infty).
$$
Thus remote sites remain below $\theta_-$ before $t_0$.
At each fixed site, \eqref{eq:heat-comparison} supplies a positive
value at time one, and Lemma~\ref{lem:amplification} gives
$u(t,j,y)\to1$. Every level in the prescribed interval is therefore
attained after $t_0$. At every such attainment the derivative is
positive, which prevents a return from above. Hence each level is
attained exactly once, at the time in \eqref{eq:arrival-definition}.
The early-time bound is uniform over the sites and levels under
consideration, and also shows that these arrival times tend uniformly
to infinity as $j\to\infty$.

Put $b_d=(d+2)/(2\lambda_*)$.
At a crossing, the profile approximation and the uniformly continuous
inverse profiles on the compact level interval give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arrival-phase-identity}
 j-c_*T_\theta+b_d\log T_\theta+\zeta(T_\theta)
        =\xi_{\theta,r(j,y)}+o(1),
\end{equation}
uniformly in the stated sites and levels as $j\to\infty$.
Boundedness of the phase and of the inverse profiles yields
$j=c_*T_\theta-b_d\log T_\theta+O(1)$.
It follows that $T_\theta\sim j/c_*$ and
$\log T_\theta=\log j-\log c_*+o(1)$, which proves
\eqref{eq:arrival-logarithm} with a uniform bounded remainder.

For two levels at the same site, this arrival estimate first bounds
$T_{\theta_2}-T_{\theta_1}$ uniformly.
Subtracting \eqref{eq:arrival-phase-identity}, the logarithmic
difference tends to zero, as does the phase difference by slow
variation over bounded time intervals. This gives
\eqref{eq:arrival-level-gap}, uniformly for both levels in the
specified compact interval.
For $(j+L_1,y)$ and $(j,y)$, the residues and inverse profile values
coincide, and the arrival-time difference is again bounded.
Subtracting the two phase identities now gives
\eqref{eq:arrival-cell-gap}.

label: lem:exact-time-change
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:exact-time-change}
The map $\sigma$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $[0,\infty)$,
and $q$ satisfies, with the same deletion convention,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:time-changed-Dirichlet}
 (1-\beta(\tau))q_\tau=Q_pq
 \quad\hbox{on }\{x:p\cdot x>h\tau-b\},\qquad
 \beta(\tau)=\frac\kappa{h(\mathfrak t(\tau)+T)}.
\end{equation}
As $\tau\to\infty$,
$\beta(\tau)=\kappa/(h\tau)+O(\log\tau/\tau^2)$ and
$\beta'(\tau)=O(\tau^{-2})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
One has $\sigma'(t)=1-\kappa/(h(t+T))>0$, $\sigma(0)=0$ and
$\sigma(t)\to\infty$. The identity
$h\sigma(t)=ht-\kappa\log((t+T)/T)$ makes the boundary linear.
Before the time substitution, the exponential and eigenfunction
conjugation gives $w_t=Q_pw$, exactly as in
\eqref{eq:weighted-evolutions} with zero nonlinear loss. Thus
$q_\tau=\mathfrak t'(\tau)Q_pq$ and
$1/\mathfrak t'(\tau)=1-\beta(\tau)$, proving the equation.
The identities are first valid in each finite box between deletions
and pass to the positive exhaustion limit. From \eqref{eq:exact-time-map},
$\mathfrak t-\tau=(\kappa/h)\log((\mathfrak t+T)/T)$; since
$\mathfrak t'(\tau)=(1-\kappa/[h(\mathfrak t+T)])^{-1}$ is bounded for
$\tau\ge0$, this identity first gives
$\mathfrak t(\tau)=\tau+O(\log(2+\tau))$. Substituting this estimate in
$\beta=\kappa/[h(\mathfrak t+T)]$ yields
$\beta(\tau)=\kappa/(h\tau)+O(\log\tau/\tau^2)$, and differentiating
the explicit formula gives $\beta'(\tau)=O(\tau^{-2})$.

label: thm:Dirichlet-quotient
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem:quotient-edge-identity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:quotient-edge-identity}
For $0\leq v\leq S$ and $0\leq\widetilde v\leq\widetilde S$,
with $S,\widetilde S>0$, the function $f(v,S)=v^2/S$ satisfies
\begin{equation*}                                       
\begin{split}
 f(\widetilde v,\widetilde S)-f(v,S)
   -2\frac vS(\widetilde v-v)
   +\frac{v^2}{S^2}(\widetilde S-S)
   =\widetilde S
      \left(\frac{\widetilde v}{\widetilde S}-\frac vS\right)^2.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
With $f(0,0)=0$, this function is locally Lipschitz on the closed cone
$0\leq v\leq S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Expansion of the square gives the identity. On the interior of the
cone, the two partial derivatives are $2v/S$ and $-v^2/S^2$, bounded
in absolute value by two and one. Integrating the derivative along
line segments in the cone and then taking limits at its origin proves
the Lipschitz assertion.

label: eq:quotient-nonlinear-residual
title: Proof
body_md:
First intersect the moving domain with the box $[-N,N]^d$ and impose zero
data on both the moving boundary and the box boundary. Let $v_N,J_N$ denote
the resulting finite-dimensional Dirichlet solution and quadratic potential. Between deletion times they satisfy
$$
 (\partial_t-L)v_N=0,\qquad
 (\partial_t-L)J_N=v_N^2,\qquad J_N(0)=0.
$$
Put $S_N=v_N+KJ_N$ and
$w_N=v_N^2/S_N$, with zero value when $S_N=0$.
For $S_N(t,x)>0$, write $R_N=v_N/S_N$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-edge-identity}, together with the degree-one
homogeneity of $f$, gives the exact residual
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quotient-nonlinear-residual}
\begin{split}
 &(\partial_t-\Delta)w_N(t,x)-a(x)w_N(t,x)+Kw_N(t,x)^2\\
 &\qquad=-\sum_{|z|_1=1}S_N(t,x+z)
                  \bigl(R_N(t,x+z)-R_N(t,x)\bigr)^2\leq0.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
A summand with $S_N(t,x+z)=0$ is interpreted as zero.
Indeed the extra source in the equation for $S_N$ is $Kv_N^2$;
its contribution through $f_S=-v_N^2/S_N^2$ is exactly $-Kw_N^2$.
The linear potential contributes $a(x)f$ by homogeneity, and the
neighbor remainders are the nonnegative squares in the lemma.

The quotient is locally absolutely continuous between deletions by
the Lipschitz assertion. On the set where $w_N(t,x)=0$, its time derivative is zero for almost every
such time, while $\Delta w_N(t,x)=\sum_{|z|_1=1}w_N(t,x+z)\ge0$ and
$a(x)w_N-Kw_N^2=0$. Hence
$(w_N)_t-\Delta w_N-a(x)w_N+Kw_N^2\le0$ there as well. At a deletion the quotient is reset
to zero, a nonpositive jump. Initially $w_N=v_{0,N}\leq u_0$.
Let $z_N$ solve the zero-exterior Dirichlet equation
$(z_N)_t=\Delta z_N+a(x)z_N-Kz_N^2$ on the same moving finite domain, with
$z_N(0)=v_{0,N}$. Between deletion times, the residual
\eqref{eq:quotient-nonlinear-residual} says that $w_N$ is a subsolution of
this logistic equation. Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed-domain-comparison} applies between deletions,
and resetting both values to zero preserves the order. Hence
$w_N\le z_N$ for all times. Since $K\ge\max a$, the constants $0$ and
$1$ are a subsolution and a supersolution for this logistic equation,
so $0\le z_N\le1$. On this interval,
$a(x)r-Kr^2\le F(x,r)$. Comparison with $u$, whose exterior values are
nonnegative, therefore gives
$0\le w_N\le z_N\le u\le1$; the order is again preserved at every
deletion.

Because $D_N(t)\subset D_{N+1}(t)$, applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed-domain-comparison} between each pair of consecutive
deletion times, and observing that every reset is nonpositive, gives
$v_N\le v_{N+1}$. For nonnegative data the kernel inequality
$\mathcal U_{D_N}(t,s)\le\mathcal U_{D_{N+1}}(t,s)$ holds pointwise. Hence
$v_N(s)^2\le v_{N+1}(s)^2$ and, using the defining integral for $J_N$,
$$
 J_N(t)=\int_0^t\mathcal U_{D_N}(t,s)(v_N(s)^2)\,ds
 \le\int_0^t\mathcal U_{D_{N+1}}(t,s)(v_{N+1}(s)^2)\,ds=J_{N+1}(t).
$$ Their monotone limits are therefore $v$ and $J_v$ by the
definitions of $\mathcal U_D$ and \eqref{eq:quadratic-Dirichlet-potential}.
The bound $J_N(t)\leq M_{T_0}t\,v_N(t)$ controls the limit for
$t\leq T_0$.
Where $v>0$ the quotients converge to the stated quotient. Where $v=0$
the bound $0\leq w_N\leq v_N$ gives convergence to zero.
Thus \eqref{eq:Dirichlet-quotient-bound} holds, including at deletion
times. To justify the subsolution property without differentiating a
pointwise limit, first integrate the finite-box inequality between any
two times $s<t$, including the nonpositive deletion jumps. Since
$0\leq w_N\leq1$, the integrands are uniformly bounded on $[s,t]$;
the Laplacian at a fixed vertex contains only finitely many neighbors.
Dominated convergence therefore passes this integral inequality to the
limiting quotient. The resulting integral subsolution takes values in
$[0,1]$ and has the prescribed post-deletion values. Taylor's lower
bound $a(x)r-Kr^2\leq F(x,r)$ on this interval gives precisely the
subsolution inequality for the original equation.

title: Proof
body_md:
The equality $v(t)=\mathcal U_D(t,s)v(s)$ proves that the sum is one.
For $s_1<s_2<t$, multiply the two normalized kernels at times
$s_1<s_2<t$. The factors $v(s_2,y_2)$ cancel, and summation over $y_2$
gives
$\mathcal K_D(t,s_1;x,y_1)v(s_1,y_1)/v(t,x)
=\mathfrak b_{t,x}(s_1,y_1)$ by the composition law.
Thus the normalized kernels satisfy the stated backward consistency. Inserting
\eqref{eq:Dirichlet-bridge-marginal} into
\eqref{eq:quadratic-Dirichlet-potential} proves the integral identity
by Tonelli's theorem. Finiteness on bounded time intervals was checked
above, including for the finite-box exhaustion limit.

label: prop:general-lower-criterion
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:Dirichlet-quotient} and
\eqref{eq:criterion-seed-inputs} give, for every $s\geq t_0$,
$u(s,x_s)\geq\eta:=\min\{1/2,(m^{-1}+KC_*)^{-1}\}>0$.
There is no assumption on the size of $v$ away from these seed sites.
Restart \eqref{eq:heat-comparison} at time $s$. Since
$u(s,x_s)\ge\eta$ and the heat semigroup is positive,
$$
 u(s+1,x)\ge(e^{\Delta_{\mathbb Z^d}}u(s))(x)
 \ge\eta\mathsf p_d(1,x-x_s).
$$
For $|x-m_e^T(s)e|\le\rho$ and
$|x_s-m_e^T(s)e|\le R$, the displacement $x-x_s$ belongs to the finite set
$\{z\in\mathbb Z^d:|z|\le R+\rho\}$. Hence
$\eta_\rho:=\eta\min_{|z|\le R+\rho}\mathsf p_d(1,z)>0$ and the displayed
bound becomes $u(s+1,x)\ge\eta_\rho$.
The last minimum is over the finite set of lattice displacements with
length at most $R+\rho$, and is positive. The amplification lemma
then gives $u(t,x)\geq\theta$ whenever $t\geq s+1+S_\rho$, with
$S_\rho$ uniform in $s,x$.

Since $\alpha_e w(e)=h$, the derivative of $m_e^T$ is positive for
our choice of $T$ and is bounded above by $w(e)$. For every sufficiently
large $r$ there is a time $s\geq t_0$ with $m_e^T(s)=r$. If
$r\leq m_e^T(t)-C$, where $C>w(e)(1+S_\rho)$, then
$s\leq t-1-S_\rho$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:amplification} to the seed produced at time $s+1$
gives \eqref{eq:criterion-inner-tube} for these $r$. The omitted bounded range of $r$ contains only finitely many lattice
vertices in the tube. At time $1$, \eqref{eq:heat-comparison} is strictly
positive at each of these vertices; taking the minimum over this finite set
produces a positive seed level. Lemma~\ref{lem:amplification} applied to that
minimum supplies one time after which all of these vertices exceed
$\theta$.

For $\rho\geq\sqrt d$, round the coordinates of
$(m_e^T(t)-C-2\sqrt d)e$ to the nearest integers. The rounded vertex
is within $\sqrt d/2$ of this point, belongs to the tube in
\eqref{eq:tube-level-definition}, and has projection
$m_e^T(t)-O(1)$. Hence
$R_{\theta,e,\rho}(t)\geq m_e^T(t)-O(1)$. Theorem~\ref{thm:upper} gives
$R_{\theta,e,\rho}(t)\leq m_e^T(t)+O(1)$. Finally
$m_e^T(t)=w(e)t-(\kappa_d/\alpha_e)\log t+O(1)$ for fixed $T$.
Combining the two bounds proves \eqref{eq:general-target}.
